channel.title: Systemic Error
channel.description: Independent commentary by Paulo Santos on politics, power, technology, and the systems behind the headlines. This isn’t a glitch. It’s the design.

item.title: The four words that explain why Trump finally blinked
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet’s answer is four words: “too big to rig.” The outlet reports that Donald Trump conceded the 2026 midterm elections after Democrats secured at least 52 Senate seats and 230 House seats—margins historian Federico Finchelstein argued were too large for threatened interference to overcome. item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet’s answer is four words: “too big to rig.” The outlet reports that Donald Trump conceded the 2026 midterm elections after Democrats secured at least 52 Senate seats and 230 House seats—margins historian Federico Finchelstein argued were too large for threatened interference to overcome.

AlterNet says courts, state control of federal elections and an autonomous judiciary blocked efforts to obtain voter rolls or circumvent election law. It also reports that unnamed administration insiders blamed Republican losses partly on the economic and military consequences of the Iran War. The article provides no independent evidence for those insider claims.

The result, as presented, is not that Trump abandoned authoritarian ambitions. Finchelstein’s argument is narrower: institutional barriers, mass participation, wide electoral margins and Trump’s own inability to translate intent into effective action constrained him.

Power met resistance

The presidency held the greatest institutional power in this account: control of the executive branch, federal law enforcement and the machinery capable of pressuring states. But election administration remained dispersed among states, while courts retained authority to reject unlawful federal demands.

That distribution of power mattered more than presidential restraint. The article’s evidence does not show a leader persuaded by democratic principle. It describes a president encountering barriers he could not readily remove and a defeat too large for limited interference to reverse.

“Too big to rig” is therefore not a celebration of institutional purity. It is an admission that the system’s protection depended partly on scale. Finchelstein explicitly notes that a one-seat difference could have created more room for cheating or illegality. A democracy safe only when the margin is enormous is not secure; it is surviving with an unusually generous buffer.

Concession is not accountability

The article correctly separates conceding one election from surrendering political power. Democrats won Congress, according to AlterNet, but Trump still occupied the presidency and retained the executive authority attached to it. Finchelstein warned that he could continue causing damage despite accepting the result.

That distinction exposes the emptiness of treating concession as redemption. Accepting a loss after threatened methods fail does not erase the threats, attempted circumvention or institutional pressure described in the reporting. It merely marks the point at which those methods no longer appeared capable of changing the outcome.

The consequential decision now belongs to the incoming congressional majority. Its members can investigate and pursue lawful accountability while legislating on living costs and inequality. Presenting those duties as mutually exclusive would be political evasion disguised as strategic moderation.

The misdirection of restraint

The familiar argument against accountability is that it may appear vindictive. That framing transfers attention from alleged abuses of power to the comfort of the official accused of committing them. It asks whether enforcement looks impolite before asking what impunity teaches the next officeholder.

Finchelstein contrasts the United States with Brazil, where Jair Bolsonaro was prosecuted over an alleged coup attempt and barred from candidacy. His comparison supports a specific institutional point: consequences are determined by prosecutors, courts and lawmakers, not produced automatically by constitutional text.

The article attributes the Biden administration’s slower approach to confidence that voters would not return Trump to office and concern about appearing political. That explanation comes from interviewer Matthew Rozsa, not evidence established in the piece. Still, the institutional failure it identifies is concrete: officials with power to act treated electoral defeat as a substitute for timely adjudication. Voters were left carrying a burden that law-enforcement institutions had hesitated to resolve.

The article overstates its case

AlterNet repeatedly presents disputed conclusions as settled facts. It calls threatened election interference an announced plan to “steal” the election, labels the reported outcome a prevented “fascist coup” and treats an unnamed-insider account of Republican losses as explanatory. The supplied text does not document each alleged threat, lawsuit, act of intimidation or voter-roll demand in enough detail to establish those conclusions independently.

That weak framing is unnecessary. The interview’s strongest political meaning rests on narrower ground: reported attempts to obtain election data met judicial resistance; election administration remained decentralized; large margins reduced the practical value of interference; and concession followed institutional defeat, not demonstrated repentance.

Calling every danger fully proven can blur the distinction between rhetoric, attempted abuse and completed seizure of power. Precision is not civility theater. It is what prevents officials from escaping responsibility by pointing to exaggeration elsewhere.

A system that survived by inches

The larger pattern is institutional contingency. Courts acted independently in this account, states retained control over elections and voters produced margins beyond easy manipulation. None of those outcomes was self-executing. Different judges, narrower results or more compliant state officials could have altered the available options.

The story therefore reveals neither an invincible constitutional order nor a single politician’s mysterious change of heart. It shows power checked by other power—and how quickly that defense can be mistaken for permanence. When accountability depends on landslides, unusually firm judges and an officeholder’s tactical retreat, the system has not solved its vulnerability. It has merely survived this test.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.content:encoded:
What happened

Maggie Haberman identified Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as the most obvious potential scapegoat for the Republican midterm defeat, but she did not report that President Donald Trump had decided to fire him. Speaking with MS NOW’s Stephanie Ruhle, Haberman suggested Trump could dismiss Hegseth, blame him for the Iran war and then present the move as an opening for cooperation with Democrats.

Haberman emphasized that the war was ultimately Trump’s decision, even though Hegseth was reportedly its most optimistic advocate and other advisers had reservations. Asked by Fox News anchor Bret Baier late Tuesday about possible Cabinet changes, Trump rejected the idea, saying the losses had “nothing to do with my Cabinet” and attributing them to a passing public mood.

She also predicted that Trump would confront a changed political environment in January while retaining two years in office. Haberman doubted Republican lawmakers would suddenly challenge him openly, although she expected pressure on them to produce results and adopt more populist rhetoric.

The president owns the decision

The institutional hierarchy is not complicated. Hegseth runs the Defense Department, but Trump is commander in chief. Haberman’s most important contribution is her refusal to let Cabinet personnel obscure that chain of authority: whatever Hegseth advocated, Trump made the decision to go to war.

That distinction matters because Washington routinely converts presidential choices into staffing stories. A secretary can be dismissed. An adviser can be condemned for bad counsel. The president who possessed final authority can then pose as the official who discovered and corrected somebody else’s failure.

Hegseth’s reported enthusiasm does not absolve him of responsibility for his advice or administration of the war. It does, however, define the limits of that responsibility. Removing a subordinate would change the cast, not the authorship of the decision.

Scapegoating as political management

Haberman described a possible maneuver, not an announced plan. Her scenario is nevertheless politically coherent: concentrate public anger on a vulnerable appointee, remove him and advertise the personnel change as accountability.

That would be accountability stripped of its actual subject. Trump selected his defense secretary, heard his advisers and exercised presidential power. If the Iran war contributed to the electoral backlash, firing Hegseth could redirect attention from the decision-maker to the subordinate most easily discarded.

The additional suggestion that such a firing might generate “comity” with Democrats exposes another familiar transaction. Bipartisan harmony can become a reward for sacrificing an official while leaving the underlying exercise of power unexamined. A Cabinet reshuffle is not a reckoning with presidential judgment.

A wipeout without an explanation

Trump’s own account was deliberately thin: there was simply “a mood in the air.” That description turns voters into weather and political consequences into atmospheric change. It avoids identifying any policy, war or exercise of power that might have produced the result.

Haberman instead said voters had delivered a clear rejection of overreach. The AlterNet report does not provide election totals, voter interviews or other evidence establishing which issues drove the losses, so that interpretation should remain attributed to her. The article’s headline also outruns the reporting: Haberman offered an obvious candidate for blame, not evidence of a settled presidential hit list.

The sharper fact is the contrast between the two explanations. Haberman traced responsibility upward to a presidential decision. Trump dissolved responsibility into mood. One account identifies power; the other makes power disappear.

Republican dependence is the constraint

The story’s central political question is not whether Republican lawmakers privately understand the defeat. It is whether they will use their institutional authority against presidential overreach. Haberman was skeptical, with reason grounded in the repeated failure of predictions that Republicans are finally about to break publicly with Trump.

Her expectation that they may seek “results” and lean into populist messaging describes adaptation, not independence. Legislators can change their slogans while continuing to protect the person who controls the party. They can pressure Cabinet officials, demand tactical adjustments and still refuse to contest presidential responsibility.

That arrangement leaves weaker actors carrying the visible consequences while the dominant actor retains command. It is not confusion about who decided. It is a political incentive structure that rewards everyone around the president for pretending the hierarchy is less obvious than it is.

Personnel is not accountability

The larger pattern is government by displacement: presidential decisions produce damage, electoral pressure follows, and the system searches for a removable subordinate. The official may deserve criticism. The removal may even be justified. Neither fact transfers the president’s authority retroactively to his appointee.

Real accountability begins by naming who held the power when the choice was made. In this case, according to Haberman’s account, advisers advised, Hegseth advocated and Trump decided. Any political narrative that reverses that order is not an explanation of power. It is a mechanism for protecting it.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Colorado Republican state Rep. Ryan Gonzalez, after losing his District 50 race to Democrat Tommy Butler, told President Donald Trump on X that he “would be more effective” if he stopped talking, using an expletive to make the point. Butler, a former Greeley city councilman, received about 60 percent of the vote, according to the report.

Gonzalez had won the seat from a Democratic incumbent in 2024. On election night, he also blamed Republicans who, in his view, campaign as libertarians but govern as liberals. While only 59 percent of the district vote had been counted, he predicted the margin would narrow; AlterNet nevertheless describes Butler as the winner.

The outlet reports that Trump responded to the wider Republican losses by attacking Fox News, its polling, and its coverage. He insisted the problem was “them, not me” and claimed his own numbers were stronger than ever.

The power was never Gonzalez’s

Gonzalez held office, but Trump held the party’s national megaphone. A defeated state legislator could swear at the president; he could not compel the president to change course, control national Republican messaging, or insulate local candidates from the party’s dominant figure.

That imbalance is the political substance buried beneath the profanity. Gonzalez’s message was explosive only as etiquette. Institutionally, it was the complaint of a subordinate after voters had already imposed the consequence.

A rebuke without accountability

Gonzalez blamed Trump for talking too much and other Republicans for governing too liberally. That diagnosis preserves the ideology while faulting its messengers and insufficiently faithful practitioners. It offers no evidence from the district showing why voters chose Butler, and AlterNet supplies no voter interviews or district-level issue analysis establishing that Trump caused the result.

Trump’s answer followed the same evasive structure at a larger scale. As reported, he blamed Fox News, hostile polling questions, and coverage of Democrats. Neither man accepted responsibility for choices within his own control. Each redirected failure toward actors accused of communicating badly or betraying the cause.

The article overstates its case

AlterNet calls the election a “widespread repudiation” of Trump and the GOP, but the supplied reporting does not provide national totals, a list of flipped chambers or seats, or polling that attributes voter decisions to Trump. Gonzalez’s defeat may fit that interpretation; this article alone does not prove it.

The framing also turns a structural dispute into a spectacle about vulgar language. The profanity attracts attention, but it explains nothing about District 50, Butler’s campaign, or the policies voters were judging. A politician’s crude post is easier to package than an account of how power operated and why voters withdrew it.

Defeat produces scapegoats

The reported reactions reveal a party arguing over who contaminated the brand rather than what governing record produced the losses. Gonzalez accused Republican colleagues of ideological fraud. Trump attacked a conservative media institution for reporting information he disliked. In both cases, weaker or adjacent actors became convenient repositories for blame.

That pattern matters because it protects the people with agency from examining their decisions. Media criticism can be legitimate, and party officials can break promises. But when those claims substitute for evidence about voters, policy, and performance, they become misdirection.

The system rewards denial

Election losses can force political organizations to reconsider their conduct. They can also trigger a search for traitors, disloyal media, and defective messaging. The responses AlterNet describes belong to the second category.

The larger pattern is not merely Republican infighting. It is an accountability system degraded by personality-driven politics: leaders claim credit when power expands, then disperse blame when voters take it away. Gonzalez’s profanity briefly exposed the hierarchy, but his own explanation reproduced its central habit. Everyone failed; responsibility belonged somewhere else.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Republican election-night gatherings unraveled as results turned against GOP candidates. At Ken Paxton’s event, attendees prayed, cried and eventually shut off Fox News; Vivek Ramaswamy’s crowd thinned as his expected loss became apparent. The article does not independently authenticate every circulating clip, but attributes specific descriptions to reporters and social-media observers.

Fox News host Sean Hannity called the announced South Carolina Senate result for Democrat Annie Andrews “brutal,” while the pro-Trump Real America’s Voice initially projected confidence using Kalshi betting-market movements. According to Laura Jedeed’s running account, Steve Bannon’s program later stopped displaying results and searched unsuccessfully for favorable news.

AlterNet also reports that Republicans failed to eliminate Democratic incumbents through redrawn Florida House districts and that commentators blamed GOP erosion among Latino voters and young men on gas prices, the economy and the Iran war—not deportations. The reporting presents that explanation as partisan speculation, not an established finding.

The spectacle is not the story

Crying operatives and empty victory parties make irresistible footage, but humiliation is politically trivial. The consequential actors are not the distressed people in ballrooms. They are party leaders, candidates, media personalities and mapmakers with the institutional capacity to shape policy, manipulate districts and tell voters what election results mean.

Centering emotional collapse can obscure that power. A supporter wailing at a television did not redraw Florida’s congressional map. Republican officials did. Bannon’s audience did not choose to substitute betting-market movement for vote data. His program did. The embarrassment belongs to the spectators; responsibility belongs to the people directing the machinery.

Propaganda meets arithmetic

The Real America’s Voice coverage described by Jedeed followed a recognizable sequence: declare victory before sufficient evidence exists, promote a convenient indicator as authoritative, minimize contrary data, then remove the scoreboard when the numbers become intolerable.

That is not merely poor forecasting. It is an information system organized around preserving audience belief. The article does not establish that Bannon or his colleagues knowingly falsified results, but it does document a broadcast posture in which confidence came first and evidence was admitted only when it could no longer be avoided.

Fox News offered a more conventional version of the same escape. Hannity reportedly reached for personal grief and inexperience when discussing the Republican loss in South Carolina. Those factors may be relevant, but the account provides no evidence that they explain the result. Instant diagnosis is useful to partisan media because it turns voter rejection into an isolated candidate defect rather than a judgment on the party.

The convenient voter

The reported discussion of Latino voters exposes a deeper evasion. Commentators reached for gas prices, the economy and the Iran war while dismissing deportations as a possible factor. The source supplies no voter data capable of settling that question, so neither explanation should be treated as proven.

But the asymmetry matters. Economic frustration allows Republican strategists to imagine that voters remain ideologically available once conditions change. Anger over deportations would implicate the party’s own governing choices. One explanation promises temporary bad luck; the other suggests political consequence. The panel reportedly preferred the explanation that required no reckoning.

This is how powerful institutions misdirect blame toward abstractions. “The economy” acts without an author. Gas prices become a culprit without a vote. Policy choices disappear, and constituencies harmed or alienated by those choices are reduced to consumers awaiting a cheaper gallon.

Gerrymandering without guarantees

The Florida result described by AlterNet is more important than the ballroom footage. Republican officials reportedly redrew House districts in an effort to remove Democrats, yet the targeted seats remained Democratic. That is an exercise of institutional power, even when it fails.

A thwarted power grab is still a power grab. The failure does not vindicate the system; it shows that engineered advantages have limits. Voters may overcome a manipulated structure in a given election, but they should not have to defeat both opposing candidates and maps designed by those candidates’ allies.

Defeat does not produce accountability

The larger pattern is not Republican sadness. It is the infrastructure built to prevent adverse information from carrying political meaning: partisan media substitute prediction markets for counts, broadcasters invent immediate alibis, strategists blame impersonal conditions, and officeholders alter electoral terrain.

When those defenses fail, the cameras capture tears. But emotion is not accountability, and losing is not self-correction. A political apparatus can absorb humiliation without surrendering any of its methods. The systemic error is treating the spectacle of disbelief as the consequence, when the real consequence is what powerful actors learn—or refuse to learn—after the votes are counted.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: Clinton strategist suggests a new playbook after Trump takes a permanent hit
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Democratic Leadership Council founder Al From urged Democrats, after their reported 2026 congressional victories, to use the 2028 presidential primaries to redefine the party around a “practical, center-left” agenda. His proposed playbook is a competitive but quickly narrowed primary, followed by an appeal to independents and center-right voters dissatisfied with President Donald Trump. From characterized the election as an extraordinary repudiation of Trump,
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Democratic Leadership Council founder Al From urged Democrats, after their reported 2026 congressional victories, to use the 2028 presidential primaries to redefine the party around a “practical, center-left” agenda. His proposed playbook is a competitive but quickly narrowed primary, followed by an appeal to independents and center-right voters dissatisfied with President Donald Trump.

From characterized the election as an extraordinary repudiation of Trump, driven by opposition to his presidency rather than enthusiasm for Democrats. AlterNet attributes Republican losses to Trump’s unpopular Iran war and its economic effects, while From cited Democratic gains in states including South Carolina, Kansas, Texas, North Carolina and Iowa.

The “permanent hit” in the headline is not an established permanent political injury. It is AlterNet’s interpretation of the election and From’s argument that Trump squandered an opportunity to build a durable Republican coalition. From explicitly warned Democrats against treating a backlash vote as proof that they had earned lasting support.

Power was exercised before the backlash

Trump held the presidency. Republicans entered the election with the opportunity, as AlterNet frames it, to consolidate control around his coalition. Democratic voters and candidates could punish that record at the ballot box, but they did not possess the executive authority that produced it.

That distinction matters because electoral coverage often treats public anger as the central political event while reducing the governing decisions that caused it to atmospheric “unpopularity.” In AlterNet’s account, Trump pursued the Iran war and made the election a referendum on himself. The reported economic damage was not a messaging mishap. It was a consequence attached to presidential power.

From also said Trump had done “enormous damage” and that voters wanted to stop it. Yet the interview moves rapidly from that damage to Democratic positioning. The people who bore the consequences become abstractions; the strategists who hope to capitalize on them become the protagonists.

Rejection is not consent

From’s clearest point is also the one most inconvenient for Democratic triumphalism: voters may have rejected Trump without endorsing the Democratic Party. He said the party’s standing remained poor and cautioned against reading too much into its victories.

That leaves Democratic leaders with agency—and no excuse for pretending momentum is a mandate. They can treat the result as permission to resume familiar consultant politics, or they can address the material failures From named: delayed homeownership, weak public education, ineffective government services and the difficulty many people face getting ahead.

His answer, however, places extraordinary faith in the nomination process. Primaries can select a candidate and clarify a message. They cannot by themselves make housing affordable, reform schools, discipline military spending or prove that government works. Those outcomes require officeholders to use institutional power against interests that benefit from the status quo.

The centrist inheritance

From presents the Clinton-era formula—opportunity, responsibility and community—as a durable governing creed. He argues that Democrats recovered by reaching beyond their base, demonstrating administrative competence and accepting the political burden of difficult fiscal choices.

But the vocabulary is elastic enough to conceal the central dispute: responsibility for whom, and enforced by whom? From endorsed progressive taxation in general and suggested that defense spending could be reduced through modernization, but repeatedly conditioned those positions on circumstances. That caution may be defensible. It also shows how “practical” politics can become a license to postpone naming whose wealth, contracts or institutional privileges must yield.

AlterNet largely accepts the DLC’s history as a template for renewal. That framing privileges the strategist’s account of political realignment and gives less attention to the conflicts compressed inside it. “Move to the center” is not a neutral instruction. It determines which constituencies must compromise first and which demands party elites classify as electorally inconvenient.

A coalition is not a permanent majority

The article’s language of permanent power overstates what its own evidence supports. From described a volatile electorate, an unpopular Democratic Party and victories powered substantially by rejection of one president. Those conditions may create an opening; they do not establish realignment.

The larger pattern is familiar: an incumbent exercises power destructively, voters impose a penalty, and party professionals interpret the wreckage as a branding opportunity. That move misdirects attention from governing accountability toward coalition management.

Trump’s reported defeat did not transfer permanent loyalty to Democrats. It transferred responsibility. If Democratic officials convert temporary control into material improvements, they may earn durable support. If they merely repackage caution as competence, the “new majority” will remain what it currently is in this reporting: a strategist’s aspiration built on somebody else’s repudiation.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Jokes fly as Trump’s DJT stock plummets to Happy Meal prices
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that shares of Trump Media & Technology Group, the parent company of Truth Social, fell to a record low of $5.05 after Election Day, when Republicans reportedly suffered major midterm losses. The stock had once traded as high as $175 and briefly reached $61.96 after the company went public in 2024. The outlet says Truth Social reported a $712 million net loss in 2025, while estimated users declined from roughly 420,000 in June 2025 to about 260,000 in September 202
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that shares of Trump Media & Technology Group, the parent company of Truth Social, fell to a record low of $5.05 after Election Day, when Republicans reportedly suffered major midterm losses. The stock had once traded as high as $175 and briefly reached $61.96 after the company went public in 2024.

The outlet says Truth Social reported a $712 million net loss in 2025, while estimated users declined from roughly 420,000 in June 2025 to about 260,000 in September 2026. Online commentators mocked the share price by comparing it with a Happy Meal.

AlterNet also cites reports about a federal investigation involving an investor linked to efforts to move assets from Russia, Ukraine, and China to the Caribbean. It does not report any resulting charge against Trump Media. Lawsuits the company brought against the Guardian and Variety over related coverage were dismissed.

The jokes obscure the power

A collapsing stock is not merely a humiliation for Donald Trump. Trump is described here as the sitting president, not a defeated businessman watching strangers ridicule his balance sheet. He holds federal executive power while his family retains enormous private financial interests attached to his political identity.

That is the central institutional fact. Internet jokes have no governing authority. Investors can sell shares and voters can punish a party, but neither controls the executive branch. Treating a five-dollar stock price as Trump’s comeuppance mistakes reputational damage for a transfer of power.

Investors funded the proposition

The people who bought DJT at inflated prices exercised agency. Whatever expectations they attached to the stock, the reported operating picture was grim: heavy losses, declining traffic and a shrinking user base. The decline did not happen because Amanda Knox made a Happy Meal joke.

Trump Media’s leadership also made choices. It built a company whose market appeal was bound tightly to one politician and then expanded into cryptocurrency ventures. That structure exposed shareholders to political volatility while allowing the Trump brand to convert political loyalty into financial demand.

A conflict bigger than the ticker

AlterNet says Trump family cryptocurrency ventures have generated roughly $2.3 billion since Trump returned to office. That reported figure is far more politically consequential than a mocking comparison between a share and fast food, yet the article devotes much of its energy to social-media reactions.

The essential question is not whether DJT investors feel embarrassed. It is how a president’s public authority intersects with businesses bearing his name and enriching his family. The reporting supplied here does not establish that Trump used presidential power to benefit those ventures. It does establish a financial arrangement that warrants scrutiny beyond the spectacle of a falling chart.

Humiliation is not accountability

The article’s framing reduces a serious power story to schadenfreude. A stock-price collapse can impose losses on shareholders and weaken a company’s access to capital. It does not resolve conflicts of interest, answer questions raised by federal investigators or constrain presidential authority.

This is a recurring failure in political coverage: translating consequences into vibes. Trump looks diminished, critics laugh and readers are invited to experience mockery as accountability. Meanwhile, the institutions capable of examining financial conflicts, enforcing securities law and limiting abuses of office largely disappear from view.

The system behind the meme

DJT’s decline reveals the instability of turning partisan allegiance into an investable asset. But it also exposes a broader political economy in which proximity to state power can become a commercial product, while coverage fixates on whether the product’s price is embarrassing.

A cheaper share does not make concentrated power harmless. The systemic error is confusing market punishment with democratic control—and mistaking a joke at a powerful man’s expense for an institution capable of restraining him.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Frank Luntz’s entire Trump voter group flipped in first for pollster
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Republican pollster Frank Luntz convened a focus group of 14 people who voted for Donald Trump in 2024 and found that every participant said they voted Democratic in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Luntz told CNBC on Wednesday that the voters overwhelmingly described their choice as a rejection of Republicans, not an embrace of Democrats. Participants cited an unspecified war, gas and health-care costs, higher prices, and broader affordability problems. Luntz sai
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Republican pollster Frank Luntz convened a focus group of 14 people who voted for Donald Trump in 2024 and found that every participant said they voted Democratic in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Luntz told CNBC on Wednesday that the voters overwhelmingly described their choice as a rejection of Republicans, not an embrace of Democrats.

Participants cited an unspecified war, gas and health-care costs, higher prices, and broader affordability problems. Luntz said they believed Trump’s promises, concluded that he had not delivered, and acknowledged that supporting him had been a mistake—an admission he called unprecedented in his focus groups.

The report says Democrats took control of the House and Senate, but it does not provide vote totals, identify the contests involved, specify the war discussed, or explain how the 14 participants were selected. The focus group documents a striking reaction among those voters; it does not, by itself, measure the electorate.

Power produced the backlash

These voters did not turn against an opposition party struggling to implement its agenda. According to the account, they turned against the president and the Republican Party after giving them governing power and finding daily life still unaffordable.

That distinction matters. Gas, health care, war, and prices are not free-floating anxieties generated by “Washington.” Voters assigned responsibility to the officials in control. Their Democratic votes transferred institutional power by changing congressional control, even if their immediate purpose was punishment rather than ideological conversion.

Promises met material life

Luntz’s most revealing observation was that these voters believed Trump. They were willing, he said, to overlook everything else that happened in 2024 because they expected results. The political transaction was explicit: tolerate the conduct, receive cheaper living and effective government.

The bargain failed for these 14 voters because the promised material relief did not arrive. Their reversal illustrates the limit of personality-driven politics: loyalty can survive scandal and norm-breaking, but rent, food, fuel, and medical bills keep arriving. Propaganda can redirect blame for a time. It cannot indefinitely make unaffordable necessities affordable.

The accountability diversion

After describing voters’ anger over Republican governance, Luntz shifted to whether victorious Democrats would police their own ranks and called accountability aimed at opponents “revenge.” That move redirects attention from the officials voters had just rejected to hypothetical Democratic misconduct.

Accountability is not defined by the target’s party. It becomes partisan abuse when standards are selectively applied or procedures are manipulated—not merely when officials investigate people across the aisle. Treating scrutiny of powerful actors as presumptively vindictive gives incumbents a ready-made shield: exercise power, fail publicly, then recast examination of that failure as persecution.

A dramatic finding with missing foundations

AlterNet’s framing outruns the evidence when it treats one focus group as an electoral bloc. Fourteen unanimous defections are politically suggestive, especially because Luntz says such admissions are rare in his work. They are not a poll, a representative sample, or proof that Trump voters generally reached the same conclusion.

The article also omits basic information needed to assess the result: participant selection, geography, the specific elections, and the war participants blamed. Those gaps do not erase what the voters said. They do prevent a vivid anecdote from carrying the weight of a national explanation.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is not that one group suddenly discovered a permanent home in the Democratic Party. It is that political loyalty built around extravagant promises remains vulnerable to material failure. These voters did not report conversion; they reported buyer’s remorse and used the opposition as the available instrument of punishment.

That creates an opening for Democrats, not a durable mandate. Control gained through rejection can disappear through the same mechanism. The institutions now changing hands will be judged by whether they alter the conditions voters named—not by whether strategists can turn 14 angry people into a comforting story about realignment.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: GOP insiders blame 'dumb' Trump 'cockroaches' for blowing the midterms
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Republican insiders blamed President Donald Trump, his White House political team, and congressional campaign leadership for a sweeping midterm defeat that included losses in South Carolina, Texas, and Kansas. Operatives singled out Susie Wiles, James Blair, Chris LaCivita, and Richard Hudson, arguing that poor candidate selection, an aggressive redistricting strategy, and a campaign detached from voters’ economic concerns produced the losses. item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Republican insiders blamed President Donald Trump, his White House political team, and congressional campaign leadership for a sweeping midterm defeat that included losses in South Carolina, Texas, and Kansas. Operatives singled out Susie Wiles, James Blair, Chris LaCivita, and Richard Hudson, arguing that poor candidate selection, an aggressive redistricting strategy, and a campaign detached from voters’ economic concerns produced the losses.

The insiders also blamed Trump directly. Republican staffers told the Intelligencer that voters were focused on high prices, which they linked to the war in Iran, while Trump emphasized renovation projects, allegations about vandals, and other subjects far removed from household finances. One operative reported shifts of 30 to 40 points among some voters who had previously supported Trump, though the article does not provide the underlying polling data or define the affected constituencies.

A Republican pollster predicted a “reckoning in Trumpworld” and compared Trump’s advisers to “cockroaches,” suggesting they would survive despite the defeat. That insult supplies the headline’s teaser, but it also exposes the insiders’ preferred explanation: the people around Trump failed him.

Power was concentrated at the top

The people named in the recriminations were not spectators. According to the reporting, White House officials and Republican campaign organizations helped choose candidates, shape the message, and initiate a redistricting fight. They exercised institutional power over money, strategy, personnel, and the party’s national agenda.

But Trump held more power than any adviser now being offered up for blame. He hired the team, dominated the campaign, and delivered the closing pitch. The account therefore describes more than staff incompetence. It describes a party organized around one president’s priorities and then surprised when voters judged those priorities.

The scapegoat hunt has limits

Calling advisers the “dumbest people” is emotionally satisfying for operatives seeking distance from a collapse. It is not a serious theory of responsibility. Wiles, Blair, LaCivita, Hudson, and campaign officials may have made consequential errors, but the insiders’ own testimony says Trump repeatedly focused public attention away from affordability and toward his preferred grievances and projects.

That contradiction matters. Republican officials want to portray the defeat as a management failure because management can be replaced without reconsidering the political arrangement that empowered it. The “cockroaches” framing turns accountability into palace intrigue: Which courtiers survive? Who gets pushed out? Who inherits the same machinery?

“Messaging” conceals the governing failure

Several operatives reduced the result to bad messaging, poor candidates, or “unforced errors.” Yet their account identifies a substantive problem: voters were struggling with prices while the administration and its campaign concentrated on other priorities. If the war in Iran contributed to those prices, as the quoted staffers claimed, then this was not merely a failure to explain policy. It was a governing choice with electoral consequences.

“Messaging failure” is Washington’s preferred solvent for dissolving responsibility. It recasts unpopular decisions as communication defects and treats voters as an audience that received the wrong advertisement. The possibility that voters understood the administration’s priorities and rejected them receives far less attention.

Insiders discovered the public too late

The reporting depicts party elites recognizing household economics only after suffering losses. Before the votes were counted, they had enough power to select candidates, wage a redistricting battle, and build a campaign around Trump. Afterward, they described themselves as horrified observers of decisions made by the same political structure they served.

That is institutional cowardice in its familiar form. Responsibility flows downward when power succeeds and sideways when it fails. Advisers blame other advisers; operatives blame the convention; strategists blame the closing speech. The people who controlled the party apparatus become, in retrospect, helpless witnesses.

A reckoning designed to preserve the system

The larger pattern is not simply that a powerful political operation can become insulated and lose. It is that insiders often respond to defeat by personalizing failure while protecting the structure that produced it.

A genuine reckoning would examine who controlled policy, candidate selection, campaign resources, and the party’s agenda—and why so few Republicans challenged those choices before voters imposed consequences. The reckoning described here is narrower: remove some personnel, refine the sales pitch, and leave concentrated power intact. That is not reconstruction. It is maintenance after a crash.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: The moment Trump’s election night watch party became a wake for the GOP
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that a Republican election-night gathering in Washington began with confidence and ended in alarm as Democratic victories accumulated. Senate seats and formerly Republican House districts shifted to Democrats, while Decision Desk called the Texas Senate race for James Talarico. Republican operatives and administration staffers described the result as a catastrophe. One organizer blamed a disastrous candidate nomination and linked the defeat to losing a Supreme Cour
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that a Republican election-night gathering in Washington began with confidence and ended in alarm as Democratic victories accumulated. Senate seats and formerly Republican House districts shifted to Democrats, while Decision Desk called the Texas Senate race for James Talarico.

Republican operatives and administration staffers described the result as a catastrophe. One organizer blamed a disastrous candidate nomination and linked the defeat to losing a Supreme Court seat. By Wednesday afternoon, AlterNet reported that Democrats had gained seven Senate seats, with Mississippi and Alaska still potentially in play.

A person described as close to Donald Trump called the result a referendum on him and said his power as a Republican kingmaker had diminished. The article does not supply the election date, complete results, or enough detail to establish the final composition of Congress.

The power was never at the bar

The operatives watching prediction markets did not control tariffs, military policy, candidate endorsements, or the federal government. They were spectators attached to the governing coalition, confronting consequences after the decisions had already been made.

Institutional power belonged to Trump, his administration, Republican officeholders, and the party machinery that elevated its nominees. The room’s despair matters only because insiders recognized that those choices had become electorally expensive.

Shock is not an explanation

The gathering’s confidence rested on the belief that polls were undercounting MAGA voters again. That was not evidence. Neither was Polymarket, which reflects wagers rather than ballots.

Treating the collapse as an astonishing reversal lets political professionals avoid a more incriminating conclusion: they mistook loyalty, repetition, and a favorable social bubble for public consent. The returns did not suddenly create the party’s weaknesses. They exposed them.

A referendum has authors

AlterNet attributes the Republican losses to backlash against Trump’s second-term record, citing tariffs that raised consumer costs, confrontation with Canada, and war in Iran. Those are the outlet’s political conclusions, not independently demonstrated findings in the supplied account.

But the reported reaction inside the party is revealing. The source close to Trump did not blame Democratic messaging, media hostility, or mysterious voter confusion. The source blamed Trump’s diminished influence and called the election a referendum on him. Even the organizer furious over a failed nominee understood that candidate selection was an exercise of agency, not an accident.

The framing stops too soon

A wake is a vivid scene, but it can also misdirect. It centers the anguish of operatives who helped sustain the coalition while reducing voters to the force that ruined their evening.

The politically important event was not that Republican insiders felt miserable. It was that voters apparently imposed costs on a governing party and its candidates. The casualties described by the article were not powerless bystanders. They belonged to institutions that chose the policies, endorsements, and nominees now haunting them.

The system rewards denial until ballots arrive

Parties built around one leader tend to treat every victory as proof of his singular authority and every defeat as an inexplicable malfunction. That arrangement concentrates credit at the top while encouraging everyone below to diffuse blame.

This account captures the moment that evasion became harder to maintain. The Republican operatives were not mourning an unforeseeable disaster. They were watching institutional decisions return as electoral consequences—and discovering that devotion to power does not protect its servants from the bill.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

item.title: Trump’s 'tone deaf' behavior draws fury after first post-election appearance
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump’s first public appearance after Republicans lost control of the House and Senate and several governorships was a White House ballroom construction tour. At an event marking installation of the project’s final steel beam, Trump praised the ballroom, described its future chandeliers and marble floors, and spoke casually with reporters. Asked whether his final pre-election address had missed voters’ concerns, Trump replied that he had heard
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump’s first public appearance after Republicans lost control of the House and Senate and several governorships was a White House ballroom construction tour. At an event marking installation of the project’s final steel beam, Trump praised the ballroom, described its future chandeliers and marble floors, and spoke casually with reporters.

Asked whether his final pre-election address had missed voters’ concerns, Trump replied that he had heard it was “a very good speech” that received “great reviews.” AlterNet reports that the address was widely criticized as out of touch. Trump also acknowledged that war and resulting inflation contributed to Republican losses, while offering what the outlet characterized as vague assurances.

Commentators called the ballroom appearance “tone deaf” and mocked Trump’s relaxed demeanor. The report also says Chief of Staff Susie Wiles could be fired after leading the party’s midterm strategy, although her dismissal remained rumor rather than a reported decision.

Power was not on the construction site

The important fact is not that Trump appeared cheerful after defeat. It is that he remained president, with the authority to command attention, stage White House events and make a personal construction project the setting for his response to an electoral repudiation.

Voters exercised real power by stripping Republicans of governing majorities. But the consequences were delayed and institutional: Trump still controlled the presidential platform, while the public was left watching him admire a ballroom. His mood was spectacle. His office was power.

Vanity as governing language

A president discussing chandeliers and marble floors immediately after voters cited the economy, war and corruption does more than look insensitive. It reveals what his administration chose to place at the center of public life.

AlterNet cites polling showing only 32 percent support for Trump’s construction efforts, though the article provides no further methodological detail. Even on the report’s own evidence, the political problem is not mysterious: voters were presented with ornamental self-celebration while judging an administration on material conditions.

Trump’s claim that his pre-election speech received strong reviews follows the same pattern. He did not engage the criticism described by the outlet; he substituted unspecified praise for an accounting of what voters had just rejected.

The convenient hunt for a subordinate

The speculation around Susie Wiles offers Republicans a familiar escape route. As chief of staff and campaign strategist, she may bear responsibility for tactical decisions. But she did not possess presidential authority, choose Trump’s obsessions for him or force him to deliver the remarks AlterNet describes.

Firing Wiles would personalize a structural failure downward. The person with the most institutional power would remain in place while a subordinate absorbed blame for an approach publicly embodied by the president himself. That is not accountability. It is insulation.

Mockery obscures the mechanism

Calling Trump “tone deaf,” a “tour guide” or the “King of MAGA delusion” captures the absurdity but softens the political analysis. Tone deafness sounds like an accidental failure of perception. The reported conduct shows a president choosing to foreground a vanity project and dismiss criticism after a decisive electoral loss.

The article also leans heavily on internet reactions to interpret his demeanor. Whether Trump looked relaxed, deluded or privately furious is unknowable from the reporting. What can be established is what he did: staged the ballroom event, praised the project, minimized criticism and offered no detailed response to the losses described.

Defeat does not automatically produce accountability

Elections can remove legislative majorities without forcing powerful officials to recognize why they lost. Institutions impose formal consequences; political organizations decide whether to learn from them or redirect blame.

This episode shows how elite failure is converted into theater. The president supplies the spectacle, commentators debate his mood, and party insiders consider sacrificing an aide. Meanwhile, the governing choices identified by voters risk disappearing behind personality analysis. The systemic error is treating a leader’s refusal to account for material consequences as a question of tone rather than a use of power.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: MAGA rages against Susie Wiles after humiliating GOP defeat
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that MAGA media figures turned on White House chief of staff Susie Wiles after a severe Republican election-night defeat, demanding that President Donald Trump fire her. White nationalist podcaster Nick Fuentes called for Wiles’s dismissal and investigation, while host JD Rucker argued that she was unfit to manage the midterms. The article does not provide verified race results or final seat totals; Fuentes’s claims about future Democratic majorities are presented
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that MAGA media figures turned on White House chief of staff Susie Wiles after a severe Republican election-night defeat, demanding that President Donald Trump fire her. White nationalist podcaster Nick Fuentes called for Wiles’s dismissal and investigation, while host JD Rucker argued that she was unfit to manage the midterms. The article does not provide verified race results or final seat totals; Fuentes’s claims about future Democratic majorities are presented as his own remarks.

According to reports cited by AlterNet, Trump watched returns from the White House residence as senior staff and Cabinet officials left the gathering. After midnight, he called Fox News and disputed its polling, even after Bret Baier said the results closely resembled the network’s forecasts. AlterNet also reports that Trump, who had spoken before Election Day about confronting Democrats, appeared afterward more open to negotiating with them.

The power is not Wiles’s

Wiles runs the White House staff. Trump runs the executive branch, leads the Republican Party and chose the administration’s political strategy. He can dismiss Wiles precisely because her authority is delegated; his is the institutional power around which the party has organized itself.

That distinction vanishes in the backlash. Wiles had publicly predicted a midterm victory, so a defeat reasonably raises questions about her judgment and management. It does not make her the sole author of the party’s record, message or leadership. Treating the chief of staff as the center of Republican power converts Trump from decision-maker into spectator.

The scapegoat has a function

Fuentes did more than criticize campaign management. He demanded ruined careers, investigations and imprisonment, while also targeting JD Vance and Marco Rubio’s possible political futures. AlterNet supplies no evidence of crimes by Wiles, Vance or Rubio. The rhetoric therefore substitutes punishment for an account of what Republicans did, what voters rejected or which decisions produced the losses.

This is scapegoating as internal discipline. A political movement built around one leader has limited room to blame that leader without challenging its own structure. Responsibility is pushed downward onto advisers, pollsters and insufficiently loyal subordinates. The hierarchy remains untouched.

Blaming the warning

Trump’s complaint about Fox News polling reveals the same maneuver. The network’s numbers reportedly anticipated his poor position; once the outcome arrived, he attacked the measurement rather than address what it measured. Baier’s response punctured the diversion: the returns were reportedly close to the forecasts Trump disliked.

Polls can be wrong, and AlterNet’s account does not establish the quality of every survey Trump referenced. But the exchange shows a familiar political reflex: unwelcome information becomes evidence of misconduct by the messenger. That habit protects leaders from correction until voters impose consequences that staff cannot massage away.

A weak frame around a real collapse

AlterNet captures the recriminations but offers little electoral evidence. It calls the result a shellacking and a blue wave without identifying decisive races, vote margins or confirmed congressional totals. The lurid details—the abandoned catering, disappearing officials and absent first lady—illustrate elite panic, not the causes or scale of the defeat.

That thin framing matters. Palace intrigue makes Wiles’s vulnerability vivid while leaving the governing record and electorate largely offstage. It reproduces part of the misdirection it describes: the story becomes who may be expelled from Trump’s court, not what the party in power did with public authority.

The system protects the principal

The larger pattern is not merely post-election infighting. It is a personalized party evading institutional accountability. Trump held the power to choose personnel, define strategy and shape the administration Republicans took before voters. His allies responded to defeat by searching for disposable agents beneath him.

Wiles may bear responsibility for advice she gave and operations she controlled. The reporting does not establish how much. What it does show is a movement rushing to punish subordinates, forecasts and prospective successors before confronting the person with final authority. In that system, failure travels downward while power stays exactly where it was.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: 'A bad look': Trump DOJ's aggressive court blitz completely collapses
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that the Trump Justice Department’s effort to intervene in the 2026 midterm election largely failed in federal courts from Washington, D.C., to Anchorage. Judges rejected or blocked administration actions aimed at state election processes, and the Supreme Court declined to disturb a ruling barring federal intervention in California’s ballot count. The administration had alleged that 20,000 California ballots were suspect, sent target letters to people allegedly con
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that the Trump Justice Department’s effort to intervene in the 2026 midterm election largely failed in federal courts from Washington, D.C., to Anchorage. Judges rejected or blocked administration actions aimed at state election processes, and the Supreme Court declined to disturb a ruling barring federal intervention in California’s ballot count.

The administration had alleged that 20,000 California ballots were suspect, sent target letters to people allegedly connected to an Alaska ballot controversy, dispatched roughly 1,000 election observers, and filed lawsuits near Election Day. Former federal judge John E. Jones III told The Conversation that states hold the constitutional authority to administer elections and that courts generally avoid changing election rules once voting is underway.

Jones argued that Justice Department leaders had acceded to the president’s wishes without a sound legal basis. He also alleged that government lawyers had failed to meet professional standards, including by giving judges answers that were untruthful or intentionally disingenuous. Those are Jones’s assessments; the article does not independently establish the lawyers’ intent.

Power did not disappear

The institutional power here belonged to the executive branch. The Justice Department could deploy lawyers, issue target letters, announce investigations, send observers and force state officials to spend the final days of an election answering federal demands.

That campaign did not need to win in court to impose costs. State and local election workers still had to divert time and resources toward litigation. People named in unresolved investigations could still be exposed to public suspicion. Courts still had to process claims one judge characterized as part of an effort to “intimidate, threaten and coerce” election officials.

The courtroom losses matter, but “collapse” describes the legal outcome more accurately than the exercise of power. The administration acted; everyone else had to respond.

The decision came from above

Jones placed responsibility on Justice Department leadership for accepting the president’s demands and sending weak cases into federal court. That is the central chain of agency: the president sought federal involvement, department leaders enabled it, and government attorneys carried it out.

Calling the litigation clumsy risks reducing an abuse of institutional authority to poor craftsmanship. Competent lawyering is not the missing safeguard when political leaders order the Justice Department into election administration. The missing safeguard is leadership willing to refuse.

The reported breach was therefore not merely reputational. A department with criminal investigative power acted close enough to Election Day that allegations alone could shape public perception before evidence was tested or cases resolved.

The “bad look” is the least of it

Jones called the performance of government litigators a “bad look,” but aesthetics are not the governing issue. The constitutional allocation of power is. Article I assigns election administration to states, subject to congressional authority; it does not give the president a general power to supervise ballot counting.

The article also invokes the Purcell principle, under which federal courts generally avoid disrupting election procedures once voting is underway. By that point, many voters had already cast ballots in person or by mail. Late intervention would not have corrected a static process. It would have altered an election already in progress.

Framing the episode chiefly as professional decline understates the political consequence. When federal prosecutors announce investigations and invoke suspected criminality around voting, they can manufacture doubt without proving misconduct. The implication arrives immediately; legal resolution comes later.

Courts contained this attempt

Judges supplied the resistance that Justice Department leadership reportedly did not. They rejected intervention, questioned government representations and forced federal lawyers to substantiate claims that carried the authority of the United States.

But judicial containment should not be mistaken for institutional health. Jones described courts operating without their usual presumption that government attorneys are behaving regularly and answering candidly. If judges must treat federal representations as potentially unreliable, every dispute becomes slower and harder to adjudicate.

The courts prevented the reported campaign from producing the requested legal result. They could not erase the intimidation alleged by one judge, restore the resources consumed by emergency litigation or prevent unresolved accusations from circulating during the election.

The systemic error

This episode reveals how executive power can be used against an election without successfully overturning a single ruling. Investigations, threats of prosecution and emergency lawsuits can burden administrators, stigmatize participants and seed suspicion while preserving the defense that the government was merely asking legal questions.

The larger pattern is the conversion of institutional failure into political utility. Losing cases can still broadcast fraud allegations and establish federal intrusion as routine. Each attempted intervention tests which officials will comply, which lawyers will object and how much disruption courts will tolerate.

A legal defeat is therefore not self-correction. It is evidence that one institution stopped another after Justice Department leaders had already chosen to cross boundaries their predecessors treated as essential. The system held at the judicial stage because it had already failed at the executive one.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: Trump official turns on Pentagon chief as blame game erupts
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened A senior White House official blamed Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth’s advice about the Iran war after Republicans lost control of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections, AlterNet reported, citing the Washington Examiner. The unnamed official questioned whether Hegseth’s projections had been accurate and said he should be prepared to explain his advice to Congress. According to the report, Democrats secured at least 54 Senate seats and passed the 218-seat threshold for a House majorit
item.content:encoded:
What happened

A senior White House official blamed Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth’s advice about the Iran war after Republicans lost control of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections, AlterNet reported, citing the Washington Examiner. The unnamed official questioned whether Hegseth’s projections had been accurate and said he should be prepared to explain his advice to Congress.

According to the report, Democrats secured at least 54 Senate seats and passed the 218-seat threshold for a House majority, with Alaska still uncalled overnight. Trump acknowledged that the war contributed to the losses but also blamed uninspiring candidates. He said personnel changes were unlikely, while former Trump aide Sarah Matthews argued that responsibility belonged with Trump and cited the war, tariffs, mass deportations and alleged administration corruption.

The power is still with Trump

Hegseth may have advised the president, but Trump held the authority to accept that advice and pursue the war. An adviser can miscalculate. Only the president commands the administration and owns its decisions.

That distinction is precisely what the anonymous official’s attack obscures. Asking what Hegseth promised is legitimate; treating his answer as the central question is not. The larger question is why Trump approved the policy, what evidence he relied on and what consequences his administration anticipated.

A scapegoat takes shape

The White House official’s remark reads as the opening move in an internal effort to relocate responsibility. Hegseth is being positioned as the expendable subordinate whose projections supposedly led the president astray.

The reporting does not establish what Hegseth actually advised, whether his projections were wrong or whether Trump followed them. It establishes only that an unnamed official wants Congress—and the public—to look in Hegseth’s direction. That is accusation, not proof.

Electoral defeat clarifies incentives

Republicans’ losses altered the balance of institutional power. Democratic control of both chambers would bring committee gavels and subpoena authority in January, giving the opposition tools to examine the administration’s conduct of the Iran war.

That prospect explains the urgency of the finger-pointing. Before oversight begins, competing factions have an incentive to fix the story: the war was somebody else’s mistake, the candidates were weak, the polling was unfair, or an uncontrollable “wave” simply arrived. Each explanation reduces the agency of the officials who made and defended the governing choices voters encountered.

The blame game is the policy story

AlterNet frames the dispute around whether Hegseth is “on the chopping block,” but personnel drama is secondary. Firing one official would not answer what the war was meant to accomplish, what Trump was told or why the administration proceeded.

Trump’s attacks on Fox News, polling and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott further scatter responsibility. Another aide’s claim that nobody was at fault dissolves it altogether. These are different versions of the same political maneuver: preserve presidential authority while denying presidential accountability.

Power without ownership

This episode reveals a durable pattern of executive politics. Decisions are centralized when power is useful, then fragmented when consequences arrive. Advisers become masterminds, candidates become failures, media become saboteurs and election results become impersonal weather.

Congressional scrutiny could disrupt that arrangement, but only if it follows the decision chain instead of the scapegoat. Hegseth’s advice matters. Trump’s choice to act on it matters more. An administration cannot credibly claim command when policy is announced and helplessness when the bill comes due.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.
