item.title: Insider warns DOJ's 'destruction' will take ‘generations to repair’
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Mary Trump warned the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division has suffered damage that could take “generations to repair.” In a YouTube video, she blamed the Trump administration and singled out Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon for presiding over a severe loss of staff and institutional expertise. A Human Rights Watch report cited by AlterNet found that the division lost roughly 75 percent of its attorneys between January 2025 and spring 2026, whi
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Mary Trump warned the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division has suffered damage that could take “generations to repair.” In a YouTube video, she blamed the Trump administration and singled out Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon for presiding over a severe loss of staff and institutional expertise.

A Human Rights Watch report cited by AlterNet found that the division lost roughly 75 percent of its attorneys between January 2025 and spring 2026, while offices closed and investigations were dropped. More than 200 former Justice Department employees separately warned in December 2025 that leaders were retreating from police-brutality, sexual-harassment, and voting-discrimination matters.

The Justice Department disputed that characterization, telling Reuters it was restoring the division’s original mission. It later announced the dismissal of more than 50 long-running school-desegregation cases, saying districts would be released from federal oversight only after individual reviews concluded they had achieved unitary status.

The power sits inside the executive branch

Mary Trump’s warning is commentary, not the underlying exercise of power. She is Donald Trump’s niece and a clinical psychologist, not a Justice Department insider identified by AlterNet as having direct knowledge of the division’s operations. The headline’s “insider” label therefore oversells her institutional standing.

The consequential actors are the administration officials controlling personnel, enforcement priorities, investigations, and litigation. Dhillon leads the division. The Trump administration directs the department. These officials can decide which cases receive lawyers, which investigations continue, and when the federal government stops supervising compliance.

That authority matters more than the family connection featured in the story. The evidence of institutional change lies in the reported departures, closures, dropped investigations, and case dismissals—not in Mary Trump’s proximity to the president.

Attrition is policy by another name

A civil-rights office cannot enforce laws without experienced attorneys and investigators. Losing roughly three-quarters of its lawyers is not merely a staffing statistic. It reduces the government’s capacity to build complex cases, preserve expertise, and provide recourse to people alleging discrimination.

AlterNet does not establish the reason for every departure or prove that each loss was deliberately engineered. But the foreseeable effect is clear: fewer personnel mean fewer enforcement options. An administration can weaken a statute without persuading Congress to repeal it if the office responsible for enforcing it is deprived of the people and institutional memory required to act.

That is where bureaucratic language becomes politically useful. “Realignment,” “original mission,” and case-by-case review can describe legitimate management decisions. They can also obscure the material result: the federal government is doing less civil-rights enforcement while insisting that contraction is restoration.

Oversight abandoned is power transferred

Mary Trump accused Congress of surrendering its constitutional authority and blamed Republican lawmakers and the Supreme Court’s conservative bloc for enabling executive expansion. Those are her claims; the article supplies no specific congressional vote or court ruling with which to test them.

Still, the institutional structure is plain. Congress controls appropriations, conducts oversight, and can compel officials to defend policy choices in public. When lawmakers decline to use those powers, they do not remain neutral. They leave executive officials with greater freedom to dismantle capacity through staffing and enforcement decisions.

The weaker actors are the people relying on federal intervention against discrimination. Treating their loss of protection as an abstract dispute over departmental philosophy misdirects attention away from those who possess the authority to investigate, litigate, fund, or refuse.

“Mission” does not answer the consequences

The department says it is defending the rights of all Americans and ending desegregation oversight only where districts have met the legal standard for release. That defense deserves accurate attribution, but it does not resolve the broader evidence presented by Human Rights Watch and former department employees.

Nor does the age of a desegregation case establish that federal oversight has become unnecessary. The relevant question is whether the underlying legal obligations have been satisfied. The article reports the department’s stated review process but provides no district-level evidence showing whether each dismissal was warranted.

The central accountability test is therefore concrete: Which matters were closed, what findings supported those decisions, what enforcement capacity remains, and who loses recourse? Invoking the division’s “original mission” is branding unless the department demonstrates how diminished staffing and abandoned matters advance that mission.

The system can be hollowed out without repeal

The larger pattern is administrative erosion. Rights may remain written into federal law while the machinery needed to enforce them is reduced, redirected, or removed. The formal guarantee survives; access to a remedy does not.

AlterNet weakens its own case by centering a sensational “insider” warning when its strongest evidence is institutional: the reported 75 percent attorney loss, abandoned investigations, office closures, testimony from more than 200 former employees, and withdrawal from long-running litigation.

The political consequence is not mysterious. Officials with executive power are narrowing federal civil-rights enforcement, Congress has the capacity to scrutinize that retreat, and people facing discrimination bear the cost when neither institution supplies an effective remedy. Calling the result confusion or bureaucratic reform would conceal the allocation of power that produced it.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: NYT columnist exposes grim warning behind a wild new political betrayal
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens endorsed Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers after losing the Democratic nomination to Abdul El-Sayed, despite previously saying she would support El-Sayed. She announced the endorsement on the Sunday before Election Day, as polling cited by the outlet showed El-Sayed with a slight lead. The break reportedly followed conflict over El-Sayed’s criticism of Israel and an advertisement released by an outside group, which El-Sayed disa
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens endorsed Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers after losing the Democratic nomination to Abdul El-Sayed, despite previously saying she would support El-Sayed. She announced the endorsement on the Sunday before Election Day, as polling cited by the outlet showed El-Sayed with a slight lead.

The break reportedly followed conflict over El-Sayed’s criticism of Israel and an advertisement released by an outside group, which El-Sayed disavowed. New York Times columnist Jamelle Bouie argued on his YouTube channel that Stevens’s decision reflected resentment over her defeat and a career-first approach to politics. His suggestion that anti-Muslim or anti-Arab bigotry also influenced her is an inference; AlterNet supplies no independent evidence establishing that motive.

The power was hers to spend

Stevens did not control the nomination after voters rejected her candidacy. She did, however, retain the institutional power of a sitting member of Congress: public standing, party relationships and an endorsement capable of generating news immediately before an election.

She chose to use that power against her party’s nominee and for Rogers. Whatever her objections to El-Sayed or the outside advertisement, that decision belonged to Stevens. The third-party group did not compel it, and El-Sayed’s disavowal makes the ad an especially weak substitute for examining her own agency.

Defeat does not confer a veto

Bouie’s central argument is sharper than the headline’s melodrama: a politician who treats office as the expected next rung in a career can experience voters’ refusal as an illegitimate interruption. Under that model, party unity matters only while the party is advancing the politician.

Stevens’s reversal is consistent with that warning. She pledged support when the commitment was abstract, retreated after losing and endorsed the opposing party’s candidate when her former rival was seeking the office. That sequence does not prove Bouie’s account of her inner motives, but it does show that her stated partisan commitment did not survive her personal defeat.

The weaker actors make convenient cover

The advertisement offers an easy diversion because it shifts attention from the official who exercised power to outsiders who supplied a grievance. El-Sayed did not produce the ad and reportedly repudiated it. Yet the controversy became the apparent setting for Stevens to abandon her earlier commitment.

AlterNet also gives considerable space to Bouie’s psychological interpretation, including his allegation of bigotry. That claim may be politically consequential, but the reporting does not establish it. The documented betrayal is sufficient: Stevens made a late intervention benefiting the Republican nominee. Speculation about prejudice should not obscure the decision that is actually in evidence.

Careerism is an institutional weakness

This episode exposes a recurring failure in party politics: organizations recruit ambitious candidates, surround them with donors and consultants, and then act surprised when personal advancement outranks collective purpose. A party that relies on individual loyalty without enforcing meaningful expectations has built unity out of professional convenience.

The consequence extends beyond one endorsement. Losing candidates who retain office, money and media access can punish voters for choosing someone else. That converts public service into leverage and a primary election into a demand for deference. The systemic error is not merely that one politician broke ranks. It is that political institutions repeatedly elevate people whose allegiance to a cause remains conditional on being its chosen beneficiary.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Trump’s weaponized DOJ is flailing in court just to save his ego
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that the Justice Department pursued a series of last-minute election interventions sought by the Trump administration, including demands to segregate ballots, set aside registrations flagged as potentially belonging to noncitizens, and threaten election officials with prosecution. Federal courts rejected or blocked several of those efforts, finding constitutional defects, risks of disenfranchisement, and likely interference with lawful election administration. In A
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that the Justice Department pursued a series of last-minute election interventions sought by the Trump administration, including demands to segregate ballots, set aside registrations flagged as potentially belonging to noncitizens, and threaten election officials with prosecution. Federal courts rejected or blocked several of those efforts, finding constitutional defects, risks of disenfranchisement, and likely interference with lawful election administration.

In Alaska, Chief Judge Sharon Gleason rejected the department’s proposed response to alleged confusion caused by two Senate candidates named Dan Sullivan; the Justice Department appealed. In California, the Ninth Circuit refused to quarantine votes associated with 20,000 people flagged by Homeland Security, whose undisclosed identification method had reportedly produced citizens, inactive voters, and unregistered people in its results. Judge Trina Thompson separately barred the department from threatening state and local officials who declined to follow its ballot directives.

AlterNet says the administration planned further appeals and pursued similar voter-list action in Washington and other states. The article attributes these moves to an effort to prevent unfavorable election results, but it does not provide direct evidence establishing Trump’s personal motive or the decision-making chain behind every filing.

Power was federal, control was local

The institutional imbalance is the story. The Justice Department commands prosecutors, federal lawyers, investigators, and the coercive authority of the United States. Local election officials possess far less power, but the Constitution and election law assign them responsibilities the federal executive cannot simply seize.

That explains the administration’s tactics. It did not need to prevail in every courtroom to impose costs. Threats of prosecution, emergency litigation, and demands to isolate ballots can consume officials’ time, force states to defend lawful procedures, and place eligible voters under suspicion immediately before an election.

The courts supplied the restraint that Justice Department leadership did not. Judges appointed by presidents of both parties rejected claims that, according to the reporting, lacked adequate legal or factual support. That is not partisan obstruction. It is the judiciary refusing to convert executive suspicion into mass disenfranchisement.

A database match is not an illegal vote

The central misdirection collapses several different categories into one politically useful accusation. A name appearing on a voter-registration list is not a ballot cast. A government estimate that someone may be a noncitizen is not proof of immigration status. And noncitizen registration, even if confirmed, does not establish that the person voted in a federal election.

Homeland Security reportedly classified 300,000 registrants as noncitizens without publicly disclosing its method. Yet Nevada’s examination of the people flagged there found none, while California and Washington identified citizens and other obvious errors. Those details destroy the pretense that the list was reliable enough to justify setting aside thousands of votes.

Calling this an effort to protect election integrity reverses responsibility. The immediate documented danger was not a demonstrated wave of illegal voting. It was the federal government asking courts to burden eligible voters on the strength of an error-ridden screening process.

Litigation can be the weapon

AlterNet’s ego-centered framing is rhetorically satisfying but analytically thin. A president’s vanity may help explain political behavior, but an ego cannot file an injunction, direct federal lawyers, threaten prosecution, or launch an FBI inquiry. Officials inside the Justice Department and Homeland Security had agency. They chose to translate unsupported suspicions into government action.

That distinction matters because personalizing institutional abuse can inadvertently excuse the institution. The problem is not merely that Trump wanted validation. It is that federal officials were reportedly willing to use public authority to pursue demands courts repeatedly found defective.

Even failed cases can serve a political function. They manufacture allegations for partisan circulation, cast ordinary election administration as potentially criminal, and create a ready-made claim that adverse outcomes remain contested. Courtroom defeat does not erase that damage; sometimes the accusation is the product and the lawsuit merely its delivery system.

The system behind the spectacle

The larger pattern is an executive branch attempting to shift the burden of proof. Instead of government proving that identified people were ineligible and actually voted, citizens and election workers are forced to answer sweeping suspicions under extreme time pressure. Accuracy becomes secondary to disruption.

That is how state power turns propaganda into procedure. Unsupported claims about “rigging” cease to be campaign noise once prosecutors, federal agencies, and government attorneys operationalize them. The consequences then fall on weaker actors: voters whose ballots may be segregated, officials threatened for doing their jobs, and states forced to spend public money resisting federal intrusion.

The courts blocked several reported attempts. But institutional safeguards are not self-executing. They depend on judges willing to enforce limits after executive officials have already chosen to test them. The systemic error is treating each rejected filing as an isolated embarrassment rather than recognizing the machinery connecting them: political grievance converted into federal coercion, with lawful voting made to bear the cost.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: 'Treason of the highest level': James Carville tears Stephen Miller apart
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Democratic strategist James Carville called a Halloween image of White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller’s son dressed as a Russian soldier “treason of the highest level.” Carville argued that the costume reflected admiration for Vladimir Putin and contrasted the episode with news coverage of comparatively minor controversies involving Democratic candidates. Carville also attacked Haley Stevens, speculating without evidence presented in the article th
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Democratic strategist James Carville called a Halloween image of White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller’s son dressed as a Russian soldier “treason of the highest level.” Carville argued that the costume reflected admiration for Vladimir Putin and contrasted the episode with news coverage of comparatively minor controversies involving Democratic candidates.

Carville also attacked Haley Stevens, speculating without evidence presented in the article that she had been induced to reverse a political commitment. He said the stakes of the November 2026 election were being obscured by horse-race analysis, tabloid material, and reflexive “both sides” journalism.

The report establishes Carville’s remarks, not his accusations. It does not independently substantiate bribery, treason, or the meaning and context of the child’s costume.

Power is not a costume

The politically consequential fact is Miller’s position inside the White House. As deputy chief of staff, he possesses institutional access and influence that a child’s Halloween clothing does not. Any serious account of his power should examine the government decisions he shapes, the authority attached to his office, and the people affected by those decisions.

Carville instead built his strongest charge around a symbolic image. Calling that image treason inflates an accusation that the reporting does not support and weakens the more defensible point: senior White House officials deserve scrutiny proportionate to their actual power.

Outrage displaced the evidence

The costume may be grotesque, provocative, satirical, or stripped of context. AlterNet’s account does not establish which. Nor does it show that Miller was praising Putin, much less committing treason. Carville converted an interpretation into a verdict.

That is not precision; it is rhetorical substitution. When evidence about official conduct is available, centering a child’s costume invites an argument over symbolism while leaving state power largely unexamined. The weaker actor becomes the visual prop, and the powerful official escapes sustained analysis of what he has done with public authority.

Speculation is not accountability

Carville used the same undisciplined method against Stevens. He alleged no documented transaction, yet spoke as though her reversal required some hidden inducement. His cheeseburger analogy supplied humiliation where evidence was absent.

A politician who breaks a pledge can be judged on the decision itself: what she promised, what she later did, whom the change benefited, and what explanation she offered. Unsupported bribery insinuations obscure that record. They make accountability easier to dismiss as abuse.

The press critique lands sideways

Carville’s criticism of false equivalence has force in principle. Journalism fails when it treats unequal conduct as interchangeable merely because competing parties are involved. Institutional power, scale, evidence, and consequence matter more than symmetrical presentation.

But Carville reproduced the distortion he condemned. He complained that trivial stories distract from grave abuses, then made a Halloween costume the centerpiece of his case. AlterNet largely transmitted the rant instead of separating the valid structural criticism from the unsupported accusations carrying it.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is a politics that recognizes concentrated power but struggles to describe it without spectacle. Officials make decisions through offices, agencies, budgets, enforcement systems, and executive chains of command. Commentary too often replaces that machinery with a scandalous image or an inflammatory label.

That substitution serves power. The public debates whether “treason” was an outrageous word while the official’s concrete authority remains poorly defined. Serious opposition requires a cleaner indictment: identify the office, document the decision, name who enabled it, and trace the consequence. Everything else is noise powerful people can survive.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: Rick Wilson exposes Republicans’ secret ‘red alert’ meeting
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Republican strategist Rick Wilson said he had been told about a private meeting in which Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and his team analyzed Rep. Byron Donalds’ electoral prospects and received what Wilson characterized as a “red alert.” Wilson said he was still trying to establish the date, possibly in late May, and offered no named source or documentary evidence for the meeting. Donalds, the Republican candidate for Florida governor, was leading in some polling
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Republican strategist Rick Wilson said he had been told about a private meeting in which Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and his team analyzed Rep. Byron Donalds’ electoral prospects and received what Wilson characterized as a “red alert.” Wilson said he was still trying to establish the date, possibly in late May, and offered no named source or documentary evidence for the meeting.

Donalds, the Republican candidate for Florida governor, was leading in some polling but running close to Democrat David Jolly in other late surveys, according to the report. AlterNet also cites anonymous Republican officials worried that some GOP voters—particularly in North Florida counties described by one consultant as “more culturally Confederate”—might refuse to support Donalds because he is Black.

The article further reports that Democrats held an early-voting advantage and that Republicans might need a substantial Election Day turnout edge to close it. Wilson disputed one estimate of the required margin but said Donalds could still face serious trouble even at roughly 1.8 Republican voters for every Democratic voter.

The claim outruns the evidence

The headline promises an exposed secret meeting. The reporting establishes something narrower: Wilson says someone told him such a meeting occurred, and he had not pinned down when. No participant confirms it. No records or internal numbers appear. Even “red alert” is Wilson’s description of what the purported analysis supposedly showed.

That does not make the claim false. It makes it unverified within the evidence AlterNet presents. A political publication should not convert secondhand intelligence into settled fact merely because the phrase “secret meeting” produces a better headline.

Power was measuring its own coalition

If Wilson’s account is accurate, the people exercising institutional power were DeSantis and his political operation. They allegedly commissioned or reviewed the analysis, possessed the party data and could influence Republican strategy. Donalds’ voters did not convene the meeting; party elites did.

The underlying alarm is uglier than ordinary campaign anxiety. Anonymous Republican operatives were reportedly calculating whether racial prejudice inside their own electorate could cost their Black nominee the governorship. That is not voter “confusion.” It is a possible consequence of a coalition whose strategists themselves describe parts of its base in explicitly racial terms.

Racism becomes a campaign variable

The Axios remark quoted by AlterNet frames the election as an experiment measuring “how racist” Republican voters are. That language is revealing, but it remains an anonymous consultant’s assessment—not proof of how any county will vote or why.

Still, the reported response is politically damning. The operatives are not described as confronting racial hostility within the party. They are described as modeling it. Prejudice becomes another turnout coefficient: measured privately, managed tactically and discussed publicly only through unnamed sources.

The numbers do not prove the theory

Donalds’ failure to surpass 50 percent in several primary counties, close polling and a Democratic early-vote advantage can all justify Republican concern. None independently establishes that racism caused his weakness. Candidate quality, regional politics and turnout patterns could also matter; the article supplies too little evidence to separate them.

AlterNet’s framing blurs those categories. The meeting claim, anonymous racial assessment and turnout figures are assembled into one ominous story, but the causal links remain allegations and inference. The strongest commentary does not need to pretend uncertain evidence is conclusive.

The system beneath the alarm

The larger pattern is a party apparatus treating the attitudes it helped organize as an external hazard when those attitudes threaten its preferred outcome. Powerful actors become analysts of their own coalition, distancing themselves from its prejudices while continuing to depend on its votes.

That is the real red alert—not the unverified label attached to a purported meeting, but the reported spectacle of Republican professionals asking whether racial resentment inside their base has become stronger than party loyalty. When political institutions cultivate grievance and then discover they cannot reliably control where it lands, the damage is not an accident. It is the foreseeable cost of the coalition they built.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: Trump’s successor is walking into a Social Security trap
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump’s successor will inherit a fiscal fight in which Social Security faces a possible 22 percent automatic benefit cut unless Congress and the next president act. The available choices include raising revenue, reducing benefits, or using general government funds, though the article does not provide a date for the projected cut. The outlet attributes a $169 billion Social Security shortfall to Trump’s tax laws and places it within a broader f
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump’s successor will inherit a fiscal fight in which Social Security faces a possible 22 percent automatic benefit cut unless Congress and the next president act. The available choices include raising revenue, reducing benefits, or using general government funds, though the article does not provide a date for the projected cut.

The outlet attributes a $169 billion Social Security shortfall to Trump’s tax laws and places it within a broader federal debt it describes as approaching $40 trillion. Former Biden administration officials told AlterNet and Axios that economic growth alone cannot close the gap.

Former Social Security Commissioner Martin O’Malley disputed the premise that benefit cuts must be part of a compromise. He argued that Congress could instead require the wealthiest 4 percent of Americans to pay Social Security taxes on earnings at the same rate as other workers. The article presents his proposal but does not include an independent fiscal estimate of its effects.

The trap was constructed

Calling this merely a “trap” risks making an accumulation of policy choices sound like an unfortunate hazard awaiting the next president. The institutional power belongs to Congress and the president: they write tax law, determine Social Security’s taxable wage base, authorize spending, and decide which fiscal problems receive urgent attention.

According to AlterNet’s account, Trump signed tax policies that reduced revenue while promising to protect Social Security. Whatever label politicians attach to that arrangement, protection cannot be measured by ceremonial praise for the program. It must be measured by whether benefits remain payable and whether the government collects enough revenue to sustain them.

The successor inherits the deadline. The officials who enacted the tax and borrowing policies helped create the conditions behind it.

Scarcity is a political choice

The central conflict is not simply whether Washington can “afford” Social Security. It is whose income lawmakers choose to tax and whose benefits they are prepared to cut.

O’Malley identifies the distributional choice directly: high earners stop paying Social Security payroll tax after reaching the taxable maximum, while most workers pay the levy on all or nearly all of their earnings. His proposed remedy would move the burden upward rather than reduce benefits. AlterNet does not establish that this change alone would permanently resolve the program’s finances, but it plainly demonstrates that benefit cuts are not the only policy available.

Presenting every option as equally painful obscures who would experience the pain. A benefit reduction would fall on retirees and disabled beneficiaries. Raising or expanding taxes on very high earnings would fall on people with substantially greater financial capacity. Those are not interchangeable sacrifices.

The magician’s framing

The weakest framing treats the coming confrontation as a generic debt crisis requiring an ideologically neutral “mix” of unpleasant measures. That formulation begins after the decisive distributional choices have already been made.

O’Malley’s criticism is that supply-side tax cuts transferred revenue capacity toward wealthy households while borrowing replaced the lost funds. Konczal and Liscow make the narrower point that constrained supply and the scale of federal debt mean GDP growth cannot be expected to erase the problem. Taken together, their argument rejects the familiar promise that tax reductions will generate enough expansion to pay for themselves.

That does not prove every claim about the precise fiscal effect of Trump’s policies. It does expose the misdirection: revenue losses are treated as settled history, while benefits become the negotiable variable.

Who will be blamed

The political advantage of delaying action is that responsibility can be reassigned. The officials who approve tax cuts receive the immediate reward. A later administration confronts the depleted accounts, the financing deadline, and demands for “responsible” austerity.

Beneficiaries can then be depicted as the source of the strain because their checks appear on the spending side of the ledger. They did not set the taxable maximum, write the tax laws, or authorize the borrowing. Blaming them would turn people with little institutional power into the explanation for decisions made by people with a great deal of it.

The recurring extraction

This is the larger pattern: lawmakers reduce the state’s revenue, allow the resulting debt to harden into a crisis, and then invoke that crisis to narrow public provision. The first decision enriches constituencies with political access. The later “solution” threatens people whose leverage consists largely of voting and surviving long enough to collect promised benefits.

Social Security’s financing problem is real in the reporting presented here. The claim that benefit cuts are therefore unavoidable is not. Before anyone accepts the successor’s “trap” as an act of fiscal nature, the relevant question is who built it—and who expects to escape while someone else pays.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: Ex-staffer says 'washed-up' Trump slouching into his 'Fat Elvis' era
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Matthew Bartlett, a former State Department official in Donald Trump’s first administration, described Trump as entering his “Fat Elvis” phase: diminished, politically exhausted and heading toward severe midterm losses. Bartlett made the comparison in an MS NOW commentary published before Tuesday’s 2026 elections; the supplied reporting does not include election results. Bartlett, who left the administration after the January 6 attack, argued that Trump’s appr
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Matthew Bartlett, a former State Department official in Donald Trump’s first administration, described Trump as entering his “Fat Elvis” phase: diminished, politically exhausted and heading toward severe midterm losses. Bartlett made the comparison in an MS NOW commentary published before Tuesday’s 2026 elections; the supplied reporting does not include election results.

Bartlett, who left the administration after the January 6 attack, argued that Trump’s approval numbers and second-term political standing were beyond recovery. He predicted Democratic control of the House and possibly the Senate, followed by two years of escalating conflict. His claims about promised projects, prosecutions, foreign policy and corruption are Bartlett’s assessments; AlterNet supplies no independent evidence for them here.

Decline is not disempowerment

The celebrity metaphor is vivid but politically inadequate. Trump’s appearance, stamina and performance style are secondary to the authority of the presidency. A weakened president still commands the executive branch, directs foreign policy, influences federal law enforcement and retains a national political apparatus.

Bartlett acknowledges that power when he warns that Trump could inflict damage during his remaining time in office. That is the consequential point. Political decline may reduce a president’s popularity without reducing his capacity to make decisions that bind institutions, consume public resources and harm people who never voted for him.

Who actually decides

Trump holds the central institutional power in this account. But his authority does not operate alone. Administration officials execute presidential directives; congressional allies protect or advance his agenda; party organizations maintain his political leverage. The article gives those enabling institutions little scrutiny.

That omission matters. Personalizing an administration’s conduct around one aging figure lets everyone who converts his preferences into government action fade into the scenery. A presidency is not a nightclub act sustained by charisma. It is a governing structure staffed by people who decide whether to comply, resist, resign or rationalize.

The comfort of ridicule

Calling Trump “washed-up” offers emotional satisfaction while inviting strategic complacency. Ridicule turns the central question from what the government is doing into whether its leader still looks convincing onstage.

The framing also treats an expected Democratic victory as nearly settled before the reported election occurred. Bartlett may prove correct, but the supplied article establishes neither the result nor the inevitability of divided government. Confidence is not evidence, and premature declarations of political death have repeatedly served as substitutes for examining organized power.

Failure can intensify abuse

Bartlett predicts that Trump will become “worse” under pressure and accuses him of ordering illegitimate prosecutions, siding with dictators and mishandling war and corruption. Those are serious claims, but AlterNet presents them through Bartlett’s commentary rather than documenting them.

The broader mechanism is nevertheless clear as analysis: electoral weakness does not necessarily produce restraint. A president facing legislative defeat can turn more aggressively toward unilateral authority, personnel control, prosecution priorities and foreign affairs. If Congress changes hands, obstruction may limit legislation while leaving major executive powers intact.

The system outlives the performer

The “Fat Elvis” comparison reduces a structural problem to the deterioration of one political celebrity. Trump’s condition is less important than the institutions willing to carry his decisions, the officials prepared to excuse them and the party incentives that survive after he leaves office.

The larger pattern is a recurring American evasion: treating concentrated power as a personality drama. Leaders eventually decline. The machinery assembled around them remains available—to loyalists, successors and opportunists who learn that institutions will absorb extraordinary conduct so long as the coverage stays fixed on the spectacle.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: The one move that could completely cripple Trump
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet does not actually identify one move that would “completely cripple” Donald Trump. It argues that if Democrats win one or both chambers of Congress in the November 3 midterms, they should pursue multiple impeachment inquiries and, if they control the Senate, block Trump’s judicial nominees. The article presents those powers as the strongest available checks on his administration. The outlet says impeachment could investigate and publicly document alleged abuses even without
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet does not actually identify one move that would “completely cripple” Donald Trump. It argues that if Democrats win one or both chambers of Congress in the November 3 midterms, they should pursue multiple impeachment inquiries and, if they control the Senate, block Trump’s judicial nominees. The article presents those powers as the strongest available checks on his administration.

The outlet says impeachment could investigate and publicly document alleged abuses even without enough Senate votes to convict. It also argues that a Democratic Senate could prevent Trump from filling lower-court vacancies or replacing Supreme Court Justices Clarence Thomas or Samuel Alito if either retired. The election had not occurred in the reporting supplied, so none of these proposed actions had happened.

The headline promises a weapon that does not exist

Congressional control would constrain Trump, not “completely cripple” him. A House majority could open inquiries and approve articles of impeachment. Only the Senate could convict and remove an impeached official, and the article itself acknowledges that conviction may be unlikely. A Senate majority could obstruct nominations, but it could not erase presidential authority or reverse Supreme Court decisions on its own.

That distinction matters. The headline turns institutional conflict into fantasies of a decisive blow. The reporting underneath describes something less cinematic and more consequential: elected legislators using powers they already possess, with results limited by which chamber they control and whether enough senators will cooperate.

Power sits with officeholders

Trump holds executive power. Supreme Court justices exercise judicial power. Members of Congress possess subpoena, oversight, impeachment, legislative and confirmation powers. Voters can change who occupies Congress, but they cannot conduct an impeachment inquiry or refuse a judicial confirmation themselves.

AlterNet partly obscures that chain of agency when it shifts into “where we come in” language. Public pressure can affect politicians, but Democratic lawmakers would make the relevant decisions. If a Democratic majority declined to investigate alleged misconduct or continued confirming Trump nominees, that would be an institutional choice—not a failure by ordinary voters to apply the correct amount of pressure.

Impeachment is oversight, not incantation

The article’s strongest case for impeachment is not that it guarantees removal. Citing political scientist Keith Whittington, it describes the process as an intensified form of congressional investigation that can establish a public record and scrutinize executive conduct. That is a concrete use of power even when conviction is out of reach.

But an inquiry only has value if lawmakers investigate defined conduct, test evidence and distinguish allegations from findings. The article lists an enormous range of claimed abuses while supplying little detail about them. Moral urgency cannot substitute for an evidentiary case. Nor should impeachment become a slogan broad enough to cover every official Democrats oppose.

The durable fight is over the courts

The Senate’s confirmation power may be the more immediate instrument described here. AlterNet argues that Democratic control would halt new Trump judges and prevent the replacement of Thomas or Alito with younger conservative jurists if vacancies arose. That would preserve vacancies, not produce liberal replacements; doing that would also require a later Democratic president and continued Senate control.

This is where the article exposes a larger power structure. Presidents leave office, but judges can shape voting, labor, environmental regulation, abortion and executive authority for decades. Senate majorities understand this when they accelerate friendly nominees or block hostile ones. Describing those outcomes as merely the direction of “the courts” launders the decisions of presidents who nominate judges and senators who confirm them.

Accountability depends on using power

The story’s real subject is not a secret maneuver against one president. It is whether a party that wins institutional authority will exercise it, and whether political coverage will name responsibility when it does not.

Elections distribute governing power; they do not automatically convert victory into accountability. The systemic failure begins when officials treat powers such as oversight, impeachment and confirmation as too disruptive to use, then present the resulting impunity as an unfortunate condition no one created. Restraint is not neutral when one side continues using every office it controls. It is a decision about whose conduct will face consequences—and whose will not.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: James Madison’s worst nightmare is coming true in Trump's second term
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that on Oct. 11, 2026, a federal judge ordered the Trump administration to stop airing taxpayer-funded television advertisements praising President Donald Trump. Two ads nevertheless ran after the deadline, including during “60 Minutes” and “ABC World News Tonight.” The reporting says the campaign violated a congressional prohibition on using federal money for unauthorized publicity or propaganda. Common Cause and two unions brought the challenge after Republican c
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that on Oct. 11, 2026, a federal judge ordered the Trump administration to stop airing taxpayer-funded television advertisements praising President Donald Trump. Two ads nevertheless ran after the deadline, including during “60 Minutes” and “ABC World News Tonight.” The reporting says the campaign violated a congressional prohibition on using federal money for unauthorized publicity or propaganda.

Common Cause and two unions brought the challenge after Republican congressional leaders declined to intervene. Administration lawyers did not contest the plaintiffs’ appropriations-law argument, according to the article; they argued instead that the plaintiffs lacked standing and that the expiring campaign made the case moot. The court rejected those defenses.

AlterNet places the episode alongside the administration’s September 2026 cancellation of more than $800 million in congressionally approved spending for immigrant services, climate programs and minority civil-rights work. The Government Accountability Office said such “pocket rescission” tactics violate federal law, while the Republican majority blocked congressional efforts to stop the cancellation.

Congress surrendered the weapon

The central power in these disputes is not mysterious. Congress writes appropriations laws, determines how public money may be spent and possesses investigative and impeachment authority. The executive branch administers those funds within the limits Congress establishes.

Republican leaders therefore were not spectators overtaken by constitutional ambiguity. They controlled an institution equipped to defend its own authority and chose not to use it against a president of their party. That choice transferred the burden to unions, civic organizations, candidates, auditors and courts—actors that can challenge an abuse only after it begins and only if they clear procedural barriers.

The administration gained room to act because Congress made enforcement someone else’s problem.

Procedure became protection

The advertising case shows how executive impunity can be manufactured without formally repealing a law. Spend the money first. Force outsiders to prove standing. Argue that the dispute is moot because the campaign is nearly over. Continue the challenged conduct while litigation advances.

The reported defense did not resolve whether the spending was lawful; it sought to prevent anyone before the court from obtaining a remedy. That distinction matters. A prohibition that depends on private plaintiffs surviving months of jurisdictional combat is weaker than it appears on paper.

The ads continuing beyond the judge’s deadline sharpen the point. A court order has little immediate force when the government treats compliance as negotiable and the branch that authorized the money declines to impose consequences.

The article’s soft spot

The constitutional framework is useful, but describing Congress as “demurring” risks disguising agency. Institutions do not become hesitant by weather pattern. Officeholders decide whether to investigate, legislate, withhold funds or protect a president.

Nor is this simply fierce partisanship “complicating” Madison’s design. The reported incentives are concrete: Republican lawmakers risk ridicule from Trump, primary opposition and lost political support if they resist him. Their submission preserves careers while enlarging presidential power.

Calling this institutional collapse is accurate only if the responsible people remain visible. Republican congressional leaders enabled the outcome by treating their constitutional authority as less valuable than their position inside Trump’s party.

Immunity without a verdict

The Supreme Court’s 2024 ruling in Trump v. United States addressed criminal prosecution and left Congress’s spending, investigative and impeachment powers intact. The article’s strongest insight is that formal congressional authority means little when lawmakers refuse to exercise it.

That is the “practical immunity” operating here: not a judicial declaration that every disputed act is lawful, but a political arrangement in which enforcement is delayed, displaced or blocked. The president need not win every legal argument if allied legislators ensure that violations carry no timely institutional price.

This does not erase the distinction between alleged illegality and adjudicated liability. It explains why that distinction can be exploited: contested conduct produces immediate results, while accountability arrives late, narrowly or not at all.

The systemic error

Madison expected ambition to counter ambition. The modern party system has supplied a different incentive: legislators may profit personally from surrendering their branch’s power when the president commands their voters.

The larger pattern is therefore not an executive overpowering a vigilant Congress. It is executive expansion enabled by congressional abdication. Outside groups are left trying to enforce limits that lawmakers enacted but will not defend.

A constitutional safeguard that depends on officials valuing institutional power more than partisan survival will fail when those incentives reverse. The machinery remains in place—the statutes, appropriations, committees and remedies—but the people controlling it have chosen not to turn it on.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Historian lifts the curtain on 'obsessed' Trump's war on JFK's legacy
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump’s administration sharply cut Peace Corps staffing and reduced USAID to near-nonexistence, dismantling institutions associated with President John F. Kennedy’s approach to foreign policy. Historian Barbara A. Perry told the outlet that Kennedy embraced the Peace Corps both as public service and as Cold War strategy: Americans working abroad could provide material assistance while strengthening the United States’ influence against Soviet c
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump’s administration sharply cut Peace Corps staffing and reduced USAID to near-nonexistence, dismantling institutions associated with President John F. Kennedy’s approach to foreign policy. Historian Barbara A. Perry told the outlet that Kennedy embraced the Peace Corps both as public service and as Cold War strategy: Americans working abroad could provide material assistance while strengthening the United States’ influence against Soviet competition.

Perry also contrasted Kennedy and Eleanor Roosevelt’s support for government action on women’s economic equality with Trump’s record of opposing diversity initiatives and favoring deregulation. AlterNet further says Trump has pursued attaching his name to Kennedy’s memorial, but the excerpt provides no detailed evidence about that effort or enough support to establish that it motivated the cuts.

Power, not personality

Trump holds the relevant institutional power here. Kennedy’s pride in the Peace Corps and USAID is historical context; Trump’s administration controls the personnel, budgets and executive machinery capable of disabling them. The concrete political act is not disrespecting a predecessor’s legacy. It is stripping operational capacity from agencies Congress and previous administrations built to carry out American policy.

Calling this a “war on JFK’s legacy” personalizes what is fundamentally an exercise of state power. The workers did not simply lose symbolic connections to Kennedy. According to AlterNet, thousands lost public-service careers, while programs delivering health, education and development assistance lost the people needed to function.

The anti-government shell game

Perry correctly identifies the selectivity behind conservative hostility to regulation. Government intervention is condemned when it restrains employers, monitors discrimination or supplies public goods. It becomes acceptable when it regulates pregnancy and reproductive decisions.

That is not a coherent retreat of government. It is a redistribution of government power: less protection against economic hierarchy, more authority over private life. “Deregulation” describes what institutions stop doing, but it can obscure who benefits when enforcement disappears. Employers retain leverage; workers lose recourse.

Aid was also leverage

The Peace Corps and USAID were never merely charitable projects. Perry describes Kennedy’s support for overseas service as part of a contest for influence during the Cold War. Assistance improved lives, but it also built relationships and made the United States more credible to countries weighing competing alliances.

Destroying that capacity therefore carries two consequences. Vulnerable populations lose services, and the United States discards diplomatic influence accumulated through visible, practical cooperation. An administration may choose that tradeoff, but coverage should name it plainly rather than treating aid as sentimental generosity detached from national power.

Where the framing slips

AlterNet’s Kennedy-versus-Trump contrast is useful but too dependent on heroic biography. Kennedy did not originate the Peace Corps concept, as Perry acknowledges; members of Congress developed it before he adopted it. The relevant distinction is not benevolent great man against malicious great man. It is institution-building against institution-breaking.

The article also labels Trump “obsessed” with renaming Kennedy’s memorial without establishing that characterization in the supplied reporting. That flourish weakens the stronger, documented indictment. Staffing cuts, agency destruction and abandoned public capacity require no amateur diagnosis of Trump’s inner life.

The larger demolition

The pattern is administrative destruction marketed as liberation from bureaucracy. Public institutions are attacked as wasteful abstractions until their disappearance produces unemployment, preventable suffering and diminished American influence. Responsibility then dissolves into slogans about government inefficiency.

It should not dissolve here. Trump’s administration wielded executive power to weaken institutions that employed public servants and delivered assistance abroad. Kennedy’s legacy is secondary. The central fact is that functioning public capacity can take decades to build and a few political decisions to wreck—and the people making those decisions rarely bear the resulting cost.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: Trump's strategy just imploded as Bill Clinton’s ominous warning comes to life
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Black voters across Mississippi, Texas, Georgia, South Carolina, and Florida were casting early and absentee ballots at rates exceeding the overall electorate ahead of the 2026 midterms. The outlet says frustration with the Trump administration, Republican redistricting efforts, and a Supreme Court rollback of Voting Rights Act protections helped drive the mobilization. Former President Bill Clinton’s supposed “ominous warning” was his observation that communi
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Black voters across Mississippi, Texas, Georgia, South Carolina, and Florida were casting early and absentee ballots at rates exceeding the overall electorate ahead of the 2026 midterms. The outlet says frustration with the Trump administration, Republican redistricting efforts, and a Supreme Court rollback of Voting Rights Act protections helped drive the mobilization.

Former President Bill Clinton’s supposed “ominous warning” was his observation that communities with long experience of discrimination have an “uncanny feel detector” for attempts to diminish their representation. AlterNet presents large Democratic crowds and quiet local organizing as evidence that Republicans underestimated that response.

The reported figures describe a potentially damaging shift for the GOP, not a completed electoral collapse. AlterNet says Texas and Florida could become competitive if the turnout pattern survives through Election Day; it provides no final results establishing a “Blue Tsunami.”

Power drew the maps

Black voters did not create the confrontation described here. The institutional power belongs to the White House, Republican officials pursuing favorable district boundaries, and the Supreme Court justices who weakened federal voting-rights protections. Community organizers can mobilize against those decisions, but they do not possess equivalent authority over election law or representation.

That distinction matters because political coverage often treats turnout as a demographic weather event. It is not. According to AlterNet’s account, voters reacted to identifiable exercises of state power: redistricting designed to benefit Republicans and reduced legal protection against discriminatory election rules. The mobilization is the consequence; the governing choices came first.

The strategy was miscalculation, not mystery

The headline claims Trump’s strategy “imploded,” but the reporting establishes only that Republican electoral assumptions were under strain. It does not show final losses, much less prove that the entire strategy failed.

What it does show is a familiar political error: officials can mistake limited public visibility for consent. Organizers reportedly kept their work quiet to avoid provoking Republican countermeasures, allowing campaigns to read discretion as apathy. That was not voter confusion. It was political agency exercised by people who understood that publicity can give a more powerful opponent time to respond.

Suppression can produce resistance

Bill Clinton’s remark is less prophecy than a description of accumulated political knowledge. Voters who connected current legislative efforts with civil-rights-era suppression were making a historical judgment about institutional behavior. Whether every analogy is exact cannot be established from AlterNet’s account, but the perception itself has electoral force.

Republicans still hold the stronger machinery in this story: executive power, state-level mapmaking influence, and the benefit of weakened federal safeguards. Yet power does not guarantee obedience. Attempts to reduce a constituency’s representation can sharpen that constituency’s understanding of what is at stake—and make participation feel less optional.

The systemic error

AlterNet’s triumphalist language runs ahead of its evidence. Early voting patterns are meaningful, but they are not final results, and a conditional expansion of the map is not proof that Texas or Florida has changed partisan control. Calling the development a “tsunami” risks replacing analysis with campaign mythology.

The deeper pattern is firmer. Political institutions can narrow representation, but they cannot reliably dictate how targeted communities interpret that act. When officials use governing power to secure electoral advantage, they may also clarify the conflict for voters they expected to marginalize. The systemic error is believing that weaker institutional power means weaker political agency.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: Trump’s $1 million bounty has Americans on the edge
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump offered a $1 million reward for information leading to a voting-fraud conviction while Republicans faced the prospect of losing their congressional majority. The article says the offer, alongside Trump’s unsupported claims about election fraud, has made some voters anxious about disruption of the 2026 midterms. Voters quoted by The New York Times feared “dirty tricks” or interference affecting close margins, while one Ohio voter argued f
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump offered a $1 million reward for information leading to a voting-fraud conviction while Republicans faced the prospect of losing their congressional majority. The article says the offer, alongside Trump’s unsupported claims about election fraud, has made some voters anxious about disruption of the 2026 midterms.

Voters quoted by The New York Times feared “dirty tricks” or interference affecting close margins, while one Ohio voter argued for photo-identification requirements. Common Cause policy director Dan Vicuña separately told AlterNet in June that administration efforts involving voter purges, identification rules, law enforcement, and the Postal Service could exceed federal authority. The supplied reporting does not establish that the election has been rigged, that the reward has produced a conviction, or that any feared disruption has occurred.

The power is in the presidency

The decisive actor is not the nervous voter interviewed for a reaction quote. It is the president, backed by executive agencies, law-enforcement capacity, and a national political apparatus capable of turning an allegation into an investigation and an investigation into an atmosphere of suspicion.

A $1 million inducement does more than solicit evidence. It creates a market for accusations. Whether any tip proves valid remains an evidentiary question, but the political effect is immediate: ordinary election administration is placed under a cloud before ballots are counted.

Suspicion is not evidence

The reward’s premise is slippery. It encourages the public to treat voter fraud as a hidden certainty awaiting discovery rather than a claim requiring proof. A conviction would establish misconduct in a particular case; it would not validate sweeping claims about an election.

That distinction matters because isolated allegations are routinely inflated into attacks on entire voting systems. The accusation travels quickly. Verification arrives later, if it arrives at all.

The article blurs its own case

AlterNet opens by asserting that Trump made clear he would “rig” the midterms, but the supplied article does not provide a statement or action establishing that claim. It reports fears, possible methods of interference, and Vicuña’s legal analysis. Those are legitimate subjects for scrutiny, not proof of a completed plan.

That weak framing is unnecessary and counterproductive. The documented issue is already serious: a president used his platform and money to encourage fraud accusations while his administration faced legal challenges over proposed federal involvement in election administration. Inflating that record lets defenders dispute the rhetoric instead of answering for the conduct.

Federal leverage, local elections

Vicuña identifies the institutional conflict more precisely. He argues that attempts to impose strict identification rules through independent agencies or give the Postal Service an election-administration role exceed existing legal authority. Common Cause was challenging the latter effort in court at the time of the report.

The relevant safeguard is therefore not optimism about election officials. It is whether courts, agencies, Congress, and state administrators enforce the boundaries of presidential power. Voters can anticipate abuse; only institutions with jurisdiction can block unlawful action.

Manufacturing doubt is political power

The larger pattern is government power being used to make elections appear presumptively corrupt. The immediate consequence is fear. The more durable consequence is permission: if enough people accept that fraud is everywhere, extraordinary intervention can be sold as protection rather than power grabbing.

Coverage should not relocate responsibility onto anxious voters, speculative tipsters, or faceless “polarization.” The president offered the reward. His administration pursued the disputed measures. The legal system must determine what exceeds its authority. The systemic error begins when political reporting treats that chain of agency as public unease instead of a struggle over who gets to control the machinery—and perceived legitimacy—of an election.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: Trump is the grim result of 239-year-old warning ignored by the Founders
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that political correspondent James Rosen argues President Donald Trump’s use of the pardon power fulfills George Mason’s 1787 warning that a president could use clemency to protect people involved in crimes the president had encouraged. Rosen points to Trump’s first-day mass pardon of January 6 participants and recent reports alleging that friends or relatives of people seeking clemency have offered millions of dollars for access to pardons. Mason urged the Constit
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that political correspondent James Rosen argues President Donald Trump’s use of the pardon power fulfills George Mason’s 1787 warning that a president could use clemency to protect people involved in crimes the president had encouraged. Rosen points to Trump’s first-day mass pardon of January 6 participants and recent reports alleging that friends or relatives of people seeking clemency have offered millions of dollars for access to pardons.

Mason urged the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia to restrict presidential clemency, including for treason. The delegates rejected those limits. James Madison maintained that impeachment and removal could restrain an abusive president, but Rosen argues that safeguard is ineffective when Congress is controlled by lawmakers unwilling to confront the president.

The power belongs to the president

The central fact is not that the Constitution contains an unfortunate ambiguity. It gives the president sweeping authority to pardon federal offenses. Trump exercises that authority; people seeking clemency do not.

That distinction matters because talk of a “pardons market” can misdirect attention toward intermediaries and applicants. The reported offers of payment are serious allegations, not established proof that Trump sold pardons. But even if brokers and relatives are doing the soliciting, they possess no constitutional power to erase federal criminal liability. The valuable commodity exists because one officeholder controls the decision.

Congress is the failed restraint

Mason identified the structural danger: a president might pardon people whose conduct could expose his own responsibility. Madison’s answer was political accountability through impeachment and removal.

That answer depends on Congress choosing institutional duty over partisan obedience. Rosen’s argument is that an overwhelmingly deferential Republican Congress has made removal implausible. If lawmakers refuse to use the check Madison cited, the defect is no longer merely eighteenth-century constitutional design. It is a present decision by legislators to leave presidential power effectively unrestrained.

Clemency became factional protection

The January 6 pardons were not an abstract dispute over mercy. According to AlterNet, Trump issued them en masse on his first day back in office. The decision used public power to relieve participants in an attack tied to his effort to remain in power after the 2020 election.

That does not establish that every recipient acted at Trump’s direction, nor does a pardon amount to a declaration of innocence. It does establish the political consequence: participation in January 6 ceased to carry federal punishment for those covered. Presidential clemency became protection for a political faction whose actions benefited the president who pardoned them.

The framing lets enablers disappear

Calling Trump the “result” of a warning ignored by the Founders is historically evocative but politically incomplete. The Constitution created the vulnerability; it did not compel Trump to grant these pardons, Congress to tolerate them, or political allies to defend them.

The Founders are safely dead and cannot be held accountable now. Trump made the clemency decisions described in the report. Republican lawmakers retain powers of investigation, impeachment and removal but, in Rosen’s account, have chosen deference. Blaming constitutional architects alone converts active enabling into inherited misfortune.

A system is only as binding as its enforcers

The larger pattern is institutional power converting partisan loyalty into impunity. An expansive pardon authority becomes especially dangerous when the president can protect allies while legislators treat accountability as betrayal of their coalition.

Mason’s warning survived because it described more than a drafting error. It described how executive power can obstruct discovery and punishment when other institutions surrender their own agency. The constitutional gap is real. The people exploiting it—and the lawmakers declining to close or confront it—are making choices in the present.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: The legal trap waiting to snap shut on the Trump administration
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet argues that the “legal trap” confronting the Trump administration is the Constitution’s allocation of election authority: states administer congressional elections, while the president lacks general power to seize that role. The outlet reports that courts and state officials have repeatedly resisted Justice Department efforts to obtain voter data, alter ballot treatment, or intervene in certification. According to AlterNet, the Justice Department began demanding voter-regi
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet argues that the “legal trap” confronting the Trump administration is the Constitution’s allocation of election authority: states administer congressional elections, while the president lacks general power to seize that role. The outlet reports that courts and state officials have repeatedly resisted Justice Department efforts to obtain voter data, alter ballot treatment, or intervene in certification.

According to AlterNet, the Justice Department began demanding voter-registration lists and confidential data in May 2025, sued states that refused, and later pursued election-related cases in Alaska, California, and Washington. The outlet says the California case was dismissed on October 26, Washington officials rejected a federal request on October 28, and an emergency motion to dismiss the Alaska case remained pending when the article was written.

AlterNet also reports that election officials were preparing for possible federal interference at polling places, including the deployment of more than 1,000 federal personnel described as election monitors. The article attributes to Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows the assessment that the federal government had become “adversarial to the states.”

The power is divided, not absent

States possess the primary constitutional authority to set the mechanics of congressional elections. Courts can enforce those boundaries. Neither fact, however, erases the executive branch’s enormous practical power: the Justice Department can file lawsuits, demand records and deploy personnel even when its legal claims ultimately fail.

That distinction is the story’s political core. A lawsuit need not prevail to consume state resources, generate uncertainty or place federal authority behind allegations of electoral misconduct. Judicial rejection can stop a specific maneuver. It cannot make the maneuver costless.

Calling this a “trap” risks making constitutional limits sound like a clever ambush. They are not. The administration described by AlterNet repeatedly chose to test boundaries that states and courts then enforced.

Decisions have authors

The relevant actions did not emerge from generalized national anxiety. AlterNet attributes them to Trump and his administration: Justice Department demands for state voter information, litigation over ballot handling and an attempted intervention in Alaska’s certification process.

The officials executing those policies retain agency. Justice Department lawyers decide what arguments to submit. Federal officials decide what information to demand. Agency leaders decide where personnel will appear and what mission they will perform.

Presidential direction matters, but it does not dissolve the responsibility of everyone who converts that direction into government action. Institutional abuse is rarely a solo performance. It depends on professionals willing to give an extraordinary claim a case number, a letterhead and an enforcement apparatus.

Losing in court can still exercise power

AlterNet treats repeated courtroom defeats as the mechanism that may finally “snap shut.” That conclusion is too comforting. Courts are reactive institutions. They generally intervene after an administration has made a demand, filed a case or forced another government actor to seek relief.

The reported dismissals are evidence that legal restraints can function. They are not proof that the system automatically repairs itself. States still had to refuse federal demands, defend their authority and absorb the burden of litigation. Election workers still had to prepare for confrontations that ordinary administration should never require.

The administration’s institutional advantage is therefore asymmetrical: it can initiate conflict through federal machinery, while states, candidates and voters must spend time and money resisting each separate move.

The weaker actors are not the source of the crisis

The article sometimes buries its strongest evidence beneath overheated language about voters, organizers and a nation “on edge.” Those people do not control the Justice Department, command federal agents or choose the government’s litigation strategy.

Focusing on public fear can misdescribe a conflict between unequal actors as a shared national panic. The consequential decisions belong to officials wielding federal authority. Poll workers preparing for armed personnel are responding to that power, not producing the instability themselves.

The same problem appears when election interference is narrated mainly as chaos. On AlterNet’s account, these were identifiable government actions aimed at state-controlled processes. Whatever the administration’s motives, the conduct described was organized through institutions, not generated by confusion.

The systemic error

This story reveals the limit of treating law as a self-executing safeguard. Constitutional boundaries matter only when officials honor them or other institutions have the capacity to impose them. An administration can exploit the interval between an unlawful or unsupported demand and the ruling that rejects it.

The durable danger is not merely one disputed lawsuit. It is the conversion of federal agencies into instruments for repeatedly testing whether states, courts and civil servants will resist. Even unsuccessful attempts can normalize presidential intrusion, exhaust the institutions opposing it and make exceptional election precautions routine.

The sharper lesson is that institutional restraint depends on human agency at every level. Courts may close one route. State officials may block another. But when federal power is repeatedly directed toward partisan advantage, the country is not witnessing a legal misunderstanding. It is watching a contest over whether limits on executive power are enforceable in practice.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.
