item.title: Trump accidentally builds the case for treason against himself
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Donald Trump, speaking at a Republican campaign rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, said Iran could “take out” Los Angeles or San Diego and called that a “very small price to pay.” The article places the remark amid a U.S. war in Iran that Trump announced on February 28, 2026, and says he had not articulated consistent objectives seven months into the conflict. California Governor Gavin Newsom called the comments dangerous and urged Trump’s removal under the 25th
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Donald Trump, speaking at a Republican campaign rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, said Iran could “take out” Los Angeles or San Diego and called that a “very small price to pay.” The article places the remark amid a U.S. war in Iran that Trump announced on February 28, 2026, and says he had not articulated consistent objectives seven months into the conflict.

California Governor Gavin Newsom called the comments dangerous and urged Trump’s removal under the 25th Amendment. Jim Desmond, a Trump-endorsed Republican congressional candidate and Navy veteran, rejected the idea that any American city was expendable. White House communications director Steven Cheung argued that Trump meant those cities would have faced threats if Iran’s nuclear program had not been stopped.

The headline’s legal premise is not established by the reporting. AlterNet argues that Trump’s words supplied “aid and comfort” to an enemy, but it presents no evidence that he adhered to Iran, intended to assist it, or committed an overt act satisfying the Constitution’s exceptionally narrow definition of treason. What the remark does establish, on the article’s account, is a president publicly describing millions of Americans and a major military hub as tolerable losses in a war he initiated.

Power without an objective

Trump held the decisive institutional power described here: command of the armed forces and the presidential platform used to announce combat operations. Congress, allies and the public are portrayed not as participants in the decision but as audiences informed after the machinery of war had moved.

That distinction matters more than speculation about whether Trump was joking, confused or bargaining. A president does not need coherent language to exercise coherent power. The administration launched the war; service members and civilians absorb its risks; everyone else is left deciphering contradictory promises of victory, annihilation and imminent closure.

California as expendable territory

Los Angeles and San Diego were not random examples. California is a reliable political target for Trump, while San Diego contains an extraordinary concentration of Navy and Marine Corps personnel and infrastructure. According to the figures cited by AlterNet, the region supports more than 115,000 active-duty service members, and Naval Base San Diego hosts more than 50 ships.

The remark therefore reduced both a disfavored electorate and a crucial military center to acceptable collateral. That is not merely offensive rhetoric. It reveals a governing hierarchy in which presidentially favored constituencies count as the nation, while opponents can be rhetorically written out of it—even as their residents serve in the military carrying out the president’s war.

The cleanup operation

Cheung’s defense did not clarify Trump’s words; it replaced them. Trump spoke about letting Iran take out two cities. Cheung recast that statement as a warning about dangers supposedly prevented by stopping a nuclear Iran.

AlterNet disputes the administration’s claim that Iran’s nuclear capacity was stopped, citing unnamed intelligence findings and continued escalation, but the supplied article does not provide enough evidence to independently resolve that question. The narrower point is already damning: the White House response depended on asking the public to disregard the president’s actual formulation and accept a more defensible one written afterward.

This is institutional misdirection. The weaker actors—critics accused of departing from “reality”—are blamed for hearing words the president plainly said, while the official with the largest platform and greatest coercive authority is relieved of responsibility for saying them.

Treason is the wrong indictment

The article’s treason argument outruns its evidence. The Constitution requires more than reckless speech that an adversary might welcome. Calling Trump’s remark treason without establishing adherence, intent and the required overt conduct turns a tightly defined crime into an expression of disgust.

That inflation also weakens the stronger case. No speculative prosecution is needed to identify the political abuse: Trump reportedly initiated a major conflict without meaningful consultation, failed to provide a stable account of its aims, dismissed its economic costs and then treated American cities as disposable. The relevant mechanisms of accountability are political and constitutional—Congressional control over war and funding, Cabinet responsibility, elections and, where lawful grounds exist, impeachment or incapacity procedures—not a prison sentence reverse-engineered from an appalling sentence fragment.

The system behind the spectacle

The larger pattern is executive war-making followed by propaganda management. The president acts first, supplies shifting rationales later and leaves subordinates to translate dangerous language into something administratively presentable. Congress’s absence from AlterNet’s account is not incidental. It is the institutional vacancy that makes this style of rule possible.

The scandal is not that Trump accidentally confessed to a constitutional crime. The reporting does not prove that. It is that the American system can permit a president to launch and prolong a war with unclear objectives, publicly designate parts of the country as an acceptable price, and expect the communications office to convert the resulting outrage into a misunderstanding. Treason rhetoric makes the story sound more explosive. Unaccountable presidential power is the more firmly grounded charge—and the more systemic failure.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: Massive reckoning awaits Trump's allies as former officials warn henchmen
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that conservative columnist David French accused Attorney General Todd Blanche of using the Justice Department to pursue President Donald Trump’s opponents through frivolous arguments and vindictive, meritless prosecutions. French cited reported efforts involving former FBI Director James Comey, Maurene Comey and Cassidy Hutchinson, but the supplied article does not establish the procedural details or outcomes of those matters. French argued that Blanche is respons
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that conservative columnist David French accused Attorney General Todd Blanche of using the Justice Department to pursue President Donald Trump’s opponents through frivolous arguments and vindictive, meritless prosecutions. French cited reported efforts involving former FBI Director James Comey, Maurene Comey and Cassidy Hutchinson, but the supplied article does not establish the procedural details or outcomes of those matters.

French argued that Blanche is responsible for his own conduct even though Trump can dismiss him. He noted that Justice Department lawyers remain accountable to courts and professional ethics rules. Former Trump administration official Miles Taylor separately warned officials against trying to decertify election results or obstruct a peaceful transfer of power, while commentator Steven Harper alleged that Blanche was positioning the department to interfere with the midterm elections. AlterNet supplies no specific order, filing or operational plan establishing that allegation.

The power is inside the Justice Department

Blanche is not merely another presidential messenger. As attorney general, he controls an institution with prosecutors, investigators and the coercive authority of the federal government. That power can impose punishment long before any verdict: legal expense, public suspicion and years of exposure to investigation or prosecution.

French’s central point is therefore stronger than the article’s lurid “henchmen” framing. An attorney general cannot erase his agency by pointing upward. Trump may set priorities and remove cabinet officials, but Justice Department lawyers decide what arguments to sign, which cases to advance and whether presidential demands can survive legal and ethical scrutiny.

Loyalty is not a legal defense

The warnings from Taylor and Harper emphasize Trump’s fickleness and his inability to guarantee protection. That may be tactically useful advice to officials contemplating unlawful conduct, but it frames accountability as a matter of poor personal risk management: do not abuse power because the patron might abandon you.

The deeper failure is institutional. Government lawyers are entrusted with public authority, not retained as a president’s private enforcement team. Whether loyalty is rewarded later has no bearing on whether a prosecution is supported now. Courts and bar rules matter because obedience to a president does not convert a meritless legal action into a legitimate one.

The article outruns its evidence

AlterNet says Blanche has “frequently indicated” plans to meddle in the midterms, yet the supplied text presents no such statement. Harper’s assertion that Blanche is “angling to thwart” the elections is quoted, not substantiated with a described directive or act. Those are serious allegations, and the article weakens them by substituting certainty and incendiary labels for evidence.

That framing also misdirects attention. The relevant question is not whether Trump’s allies face a “massive reckoning,” which the reporting cannot promise. It is what identifiable decisions officials made, what legal authority they invoked and what checks actually constrained them. Accountability is a process requiring evidence, jurisdiction and institutional will—not an inevitable plot twist.

Personalized power, institutional damage

The pattern described by French is the conversion of public law enforcement into personalized presidential power: allies receive discretion while opponents receive scrutiny. The supplied reporting does not prove every allegation attached to that pattern, but it identifies the correct locus of responsibility. A president may demand submission; officials with legal authority decide whether to provide it.

The lasting consequence is not simply danger to individual targets. Selective or weakly grounded prosecutions can teach the bureaucracy that legal judgment is subordinate to political loyalty and teach the public that federal cases are factional weapons. Once that expectation takes hold, even legitimate enforcement inherits the distrust created by officials who treated institutional power as personal service.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Trump’s Epstein file blunder just raised ‘Pizzagate’ from the dead
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump’s refusal to fully release the Jeffrey Epstein files has helped revive Pizzagate, the discredited conspiracy theory falsely accusing Hillary Clinton’s 2016 campaign of operating a child-trafficking ring through Washington’s Comet Ping Pong pizzeria. The article relies chiefly on journalist Anna Merlan’s argument that documented elite associations with Epstein give conspiracists real abuses and relationships to distort into a fabricated n
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump’s refusal to fully release the Jeffrey Epstein files has helped revive Pizzagate, the discredited conspiracy theory falsely accusing Hillary Clinton’s 2016 campaign of operating a child-trafficking ring through Washington’s Comet Ping Pong pizzeria. The article relies chiefly on journalist Anna Merlan’s argument that documented elite associations with Epstein give conspiracists real abuses and relationships to distort into a fabricated narrative.

Epstein pleaded guilty in 2008 to state charges of soliciting a minor for prostitution under a deal that avoided federal prosecution. He later maintained relationships with prominent figures across politics, business, academia, and entertainment. AlterNet also cites Republican Sen. Mike Lee’s December repost of a video from Ian Carroll, whom HuffPost journalist Yashar Ali described as a conspiracy theorist who regularly spreads neo-Nazi propaganda. Lee said Carroll raised “legitimate questions.”

The excerpt, however, does not identify which Epstein records Trump withheld, what disclosure decision he made, or what authority governed their release. Its central causal claim—that Trump’s handling revived Pizzagate—is Merlan’s analysis, not a result established by evidence presented here.

Power is not a pizza parlor

The proven institutional failure in this story did not occur at Comet Ping Pong. It occurred when Epstein received unusually favorable treatment in 2008 and then retained access to wealthy, famous, and politically connected people despite his conviction and mounting allegations.

That is where scrutiny belongs: prosecutors, political officials, influential associates, and institutions capable of granting access, protection, or leniency. Pizzagate redirects attention from identifiable decisions by powerful people toward an invented criminal enterprise attached to a restaurant and partisan enemies. A gunman eventually attacked that restaurant. No one was injured, but the episode demonstrated that fictional accusations can produce physical danger for people with no institutional control over the abuses being invoked.

Secrecy supplies the propagandists

If Trump controlled records that could lawfully be released and declined to release them, that decision belongs to him. But AlterNet’s framing outruns its own evidence by calling the episode a “blunder” without explaining what was withheld or why. The omission matters because “bungling” converts an exercise of presidential power into mere incompetence before the article has established either the underlying decision or its rationale.

Opacity nevertheless has a predictable consequence: it creates room for political entrepreneurs to replace missing facts with insinuation. That does not validate Pizzagate. It shows why officials cannot exploit Epstein-related suspicion and then act surprised when conspiracists use unresolved questions as raw material.

A senator launders insinuation

Lee did more than encounter fringe material. According to the reporting, he distributed Carroll’s video and bestowed senatorial legitimacy on it by calling its questions legitimate. His disclaimer that he did not know Carroll did not neutralize that choice. A United States senator has greater reach, authority, and responsibility than the online personality whose content he amplifies.

Carroll’s rhetorical move was simple: because Epstein trafficked in elite access and was convicted of a sex offense involving a minor, perhaps Pizzagate was directionally correct. It was not. Evidence that powerful people associated with Epstein does not prove that Clinton’s campaign ran a trafficking operation from a Washington restaurant. Collapsing those claims is not investigation. It is guilt by atmosphere.

The convenient collapse of distinctions

The flight logs and social contacts listed by Merlan establish association, not identical conduct. The article names Bill Clinton, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., then-Prince Andrew, Kevin Spacey, Trump, and Bill Gates in connection with Epstein’s planes or social orbit. Those facts may justify scrutiny, but they do not by themselves establish participation in Epstein’s crimes.

Conspiracy politics thrives by erasing that distinction. It mixes convictions, allegations, travel records, friendships, rumors, and partisan targets into one suggestive cloud. The result protects power more often than it exposes it: documented prosecutorial favoritism and specific institutional failures disappear beneath an unlimited theory in which everyone is implicated and nothing must be proved.

The system behind the spectacle

The larger pattern is not that Pizzagate was secretly vindicated. It is that elite impunity creates justified distrust, while politicians and propagandists redirect that distrust into claims too indiscriminate to impose accountability on anyone.

Officials possess the power to disclose records lawfully, investigate specific conduct, explain prosecutorial decisions, and distinguish evidence from insinuation. When they substitute opacity or amplification, weaker actors absorb the danger while powerful institutions escape precise examination. Conspiracy theory is useful to that arrangement: it turns a traceable failure of law and political power into an endless carnival of suspicion.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

item.title: End of 'bellyaching': Trump's swamp talk becomes a nightmare
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Donald Trump’s promise to “drain the swamp” has collided with growing public concern about government corruption. The article cites New Yorker writer Ruth Marcus, who argues that corruption could move from routine “bellyaching” to an issue that changes votes because economic strain makes
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Donald Trump’s promise to “drain the swamp” has collided with growing public concern about government corruption. A Fox News poll released in mid-October found 88 percent of voters extremely or very concerned about corruption, ranking it above inflation, gasoline prices, and health care.

The article cites New Yorker writer Ruth Marcus, who argues that corruption could move from routine “bellyaching” to an issue that changes votes because economic strain makes political self-dealing harder to tolerate. Democrats are emphasizing Trump-related corruption in Senate contests including North Carolina, Maine, and Texas, while Republican strategist Bryan Lanza told CNN that discussing ordinarily safe Mississippi suggested extraordinary electoral trouble.

AlterNet also cites former Labor Secretary Robert Reich’s argument that Trump’s tariffs increased household costs by an estimated $1,100 annually, based on the Budget Lab at Yale. Reich further alleged that Trump used tariff waivers and carve-outs to reward helpful companies and industries; the supplied reporting does not independently establish that allegation.

The power is in the exemptions

The central political issue is not whether voters dislike “corruption.” Nearly everyone does, which is why the word is cheap. The consequential question is who possesses the authority to impose costs and selectively relieve them.

Trump holds the presidency described in the article. His administration therefore controls policy decisions with material consequences for households and businesses. If exemptions from tariffs are distributed selectively, the important actors are not consumers paying higher prices. They are the officials deciding who must absorb the policy and who receives an escape hatch.

That is where institutional power becomes patronage risk: a broadly imposed burden paired with discretionary relief. Reich alleges favoritism, but AlterNet supplies no cases proving a bargain between political support and specific waivers. The structure nevertheless deserves scrutiny because it concentrates leverage in the executive branch.

“Swamp” was always an instrument

Trump’s 2016 slogan converted systemic corruption into a story about an outsider confronting Washington. That framing concealed a basic contradiction: anyone elected president does not remain outside the system. The office commands the executive branch and can shape enforcement, trade policy, appointments, and access.

The promise also treated corruption as cultural grime rather than an arrangement of authority and incentives. That makes failure easy to obscure. A politician can denounce “the swamp” indefinitely while expanding executive discretion—the very condition that allows favoritism to flourish.

Marcus is right that corruption rhetoric can substitute for a legislative program. But that observation should not flatten the distinction between opportunistic messaging and conduct by officials who actually wield state power. Opposition advertising may be cynical or thin. It does not impose tariffs or grant exemptions.

Economic pain changes the audience

The reported polling does not prove why corruption has risen as a concern, nor does it predict an election result. Marcus offers a plausible political mechanism: voters facing high grocery bills may become less tolerant of apparent self-dealing.

That matters because corruption is often reported as an ethics story detached from ordinary life. In practice, government favoritism determines who pays, who profits, who receives access, and who gets relief. Tariffs are a clear example of that distributional power: the article reports an estimated annual household cost, while Reich alleges politically useful carve-outs for selected businesses.

The nightmare for Republicans is therefore not merely that Democrats found an effective accusation. It is that economic pressure can make an otherwise abstract abuse of power legible. People notice privilege more sharply when they are financing it.

The electoral warning

Lanza’s Mississippi remark is evidence of Republican anxiety, not proof that the party is doomed. AlterNet’s stronger formulation outruns the quotation. A strategist expressing alarm about the electoral map establishes concern; it does not establish the final outcome of races the article describes as upcoming.

That distinction does not weaken the political signal. When a party must spend attention defending terrain it normally treats as secure, its coalition is under strain. The corruption issue may be contributing to that strain, but the supplied evidence cannot separate it from prices, tariffs, or broader dissatisfaction.

The system behind the scandal

The larger pattern is a political economy built on concentrated discretion and diffuse costs. Presidents can impose policies affecting millions, while the benefits of access or exemption accrue narrowly. Voters experience the bill; favored interests know whom to petition.

“Drain the swamp” misdirected attention from that machinery toward a theatrical war against Washington. The useful question is not whether a leader sounds disgusted by corruption. It is whether public power has been constrained, decisions made transparent, and discretionary favors subjected to enforceable rules. Without those limits, anti-corruption language becomes another asset controlled by the people with the greatest capacity to corrupt the system.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: The longest decade of our lives
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet columnist D. Earl Stephens argues that the two years since Donald Trump’s reported 2024 reelection have felt like “the longest decade” because opponents have remained emotionally and politically engaged rather than tuning out. Writing ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections, he urges those readers to vote Republicans out of office and presents the election as their clearest available means of restraining the administration. Stephens traces his anger through Trump’s 2024 victo
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet columnist D. Earl Stephens argues that the two years since Donald Trump’s reported 2024 reelection have felt like “the longest decade” because opponents have remained emotionally and politically engaged rather than tuning out. Writing ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections, he urges those readers to vote Republicans out of office and presents the election as their clearest available means of restraining the administration.

Stephens traces his anger through Trump’s 2024 victory, the January 6, 2021 attack on the Capitol, and what he regards as the Biden administration’s failure to secure timely accountability. He also levels sweeping allegations about actions during Trump’s new term, but the column supplies little supporting evidence for those claims. Its central message is exhortation, not reported verification: Trump’s opponents were right to resist, Stephens says, and must keep doing so regardless of Tuesday’s results.

Power is not evenly distributed

The column’s readers may possess votes, organizing capacity, and the ability to sustain opposition. They do not control the executive branch, Congress, federal prosecution, or the Supreme Court. Those institutions hold the power to enforce laws, deploy government personnel, shape elections, and determine whether official misconduct produces consequences.

Stephens correctly locates much of that power among Trump, Republican officials, and conservative justices. But his repeated use of “we” sometimes blurs the decisive distinction between citizens who failed to stop an outcome and officials empowered to cause or prevent it. A voter can protest impunity. An attorney general can decide whether and how aggressively to pursue a federal case. Those are not comparable forms of agency.

The decision behind the impunity

Stephens reserves particular fury for Joe Biden and former Attorney General Merrick Garland. His argument is that delayed accountability after January 6 allowed Trump to return stronger. The column, however, does not establish which prosecutorial decisions Garland made, what legal constraints applied, or whether different timing would have prevented Trump’s return. The causal claim is forceful but not demonstrated here.

The underlying institutional criticism remains sharper than the personal denunciation: a system that moves cautiously against powerful officeholders can make delay function like protection, whatever the stated rationale. Procedures imposed in the name of institutional legitimacy lose credibility when their practical result is that accountability arrives too late to affect political power.

Anger is not evidence

The article is most persuasive when it identifies officials, offices, and failures of accountability. It is weakest when accusation substitutes for documentation. Claims that people were “murdered in our streets,” troops sent to die “for his profit,” or environmental protections destroyed for personal gain require dates, decisions, victims, legal records, and evidence of motive. None is provided in the supplied column.

That omission matters politically. Trump’s opponents do not strengthen their case by treating outrage as self-authenticating. A publication confronting abuses of power must document executive orders, appropriations, court rulings, deployments, enforcement actions, and measurable consequences. Otherwise, a column condemning propaganda adopts one of propaganda’s central habits: demanding that emotional certainty carry facts it has not established.

Voters are responsible, but not sovereign

Stephens directs justified attention toward people who knowingly supported Trump after January 6. Elections confer power, and voters are not absolved from the foreseeable consequences of their choices. But the column’s fixation on their moral character risks making ordinary supporters the final explanation for an organized political project.

Party leaders recruited candidates, financed campaigns, normalized election denial, and converted personal loyalty into institutional discipline. Wealthy donors supplied resources. Media organizations supplied attention and euphemism. Officeholders possessed opportunities to impose consequences and often declined to do so. Blaming voters without mapping that machinery mistakes the fuel for the engine.

The system rewards delay

The larger pattern is not simply that one faction behaves badly while another suffers nobly. It is that American institutions repeatedly grant powerful actors time, procedural deference, and opportunities for rehabilitation that weaker defendants rarely receive. The public is then told that the resulting impunity reflects complexity, polarization, or national division—as though no identifiable official made a choice.

Stephens’s column captures the exhaustion produced by that cycle, but exhaustion is not the analysis. The analysis is that power protects itself through delay, diffused responsibility, and selective caution. Elections can interrupt that protection, but voting alone does not explain who built it, who maintained it, or why accountability so often arrives after its political value has expired.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: GOP’s final dash to pass Trump’s agenda set to crash into reality
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that congressional Republicans are divided over whether to use a post-midterm lame-duck session to advance more of President Donald Trump’s agenda before January 2027. Citing The Hill, it says one Republican faction wants an extended session and another reconciliation package, which could pass partisan priorities without Democratic votes. That plan may fail even if Republicans lose control of Congress. The Hill’s reporters say defeated or discouraged lawmakers may
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that congressional Republicans are divided over whether to use a post-midterm lame-duck session to advance more of President Donald Trump’s agenda before January 2027. Citing The Hill, it says one Republican faction wants an extended session and another reconciliation package, which could pass partisan priorities without Democratic votes.

That plan may fail even if Republicans lose control of Congress. The Hill’s reporters say defeated or discouraged lawmakers may leave Washington as the December holidays approach, while House attendance problems could deprive the party of the votes needed to pass legislation. Republican strategist Douglas Heye separately argued in December that Trump would retain political influence even under divided government and could complicate the ambitions of potential 2028 nominees such as JD Vance or Marco Rubio.

Power before the handover

The institutional power belongs to the Republican congressional majority while it lasts. Its leaders control the schedule, and its members control whether legislation advances. Democrats’ expected gains remain projections; they have not produced the outcome described here.

The operative question is therefore not whether Trump can personally will another package into law. It is whether Republican lawmakers will use their remaining procedural authority after an election that may reject their continued control.

The obstacle is the governing party

The reporting identifies no Democratic mechanism blocking this proposed final push. Reconciliation is attractive precisely because it can bypass the need for Democratic support. If the effort collapses, the immediate cause would be Republican disagreement, absenteeism, or unwillingness to remain in Washington long enough to vote.

Calling that collision “reality” risks making a collection of choices sound like weather. Lawmakers decide whether to convene, negotiate and appear for votes. Holiday impatience is not an institutional force. It is a priority expressed through absence.

A mandate treated as a deadline

The most revealing feature of the plan is its timing. Some Republicans are contemplating using the interval between an election and the seating of a new Congress to enact policies that could not pass once the voters’ newly chosen representatives take office.

That would be lawful use of existing authority, based on the account provided. It would also expose a stark political logic: an anticipated loss of power becomes a reason to accelerate partisan legislation, not reconsider it. Electoral accountability is treated as an expiration clock.

Influence is not legislative control

Heye’s warning that Trump may never become a conventional lame duck shifts the subject from governing power to media and party power. A president facing an opposition-controlled chamber could lose the ability to move major legislation while retaining the ability to command attention, shape Republican primaries and disrupt succession plans.

Those are distinct forms of power. The article blurs them by asking whether Trump would truly be a lame duck. Congress can obstruct his legislative agenda even as Republican politicians remain organized around his capacity to “make news.” Losing a congressional majority would constrain the presidency; it would not necessarily free the party from Trump’s influence.

The system rewards the last-minute raid

This story reveals a recurring pattern in American government: departing majorities retain substantial authority after voters have acted but before power formally changes hands. The lame-duck period creates an opening for consequential decisions by legislators who may already have been rejected or retired.

The deeper failure is not confusion about what Republicans might do. It is coverage that turns identifiable decisions into a suspense story about momentum, morale and holiday calendars. Republican leaders would choose whether to force a final package. Republican members would choose whether to supply the votes. If the attempt succeeds, they own the policy consequences. If it fails, Democrats did not stop it; the governing majority failed to exercise the power it still held.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: Trump’s top MAGA evangelical is already jumping ship
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet, citing the Guardian, reports that Christian nationalist organizer Lance Wallnau has stopped mobilizing followers around the approaching midterm elections and is instead discussing personal discipline, movement succession and a “post-Trump infrastructure.” At a recent partner event in the Dallas–Fort Worth area, he reportedly devoted three sessions to subjects including El Salvador’s prisons and school boards without mentioning the elections, then little more than three we
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet, citing the Guardian, reports that Christian nationalist organizer Lance Wallnau has stopped mobilizing followers around the approaching midterm elections and is instead discussing personal discipline, movement succession and a “post-Trump infrastructure.” At a recent partner event in the Dallas–Fort Worth area, he reportedly devoted three sessions to subjects including El Salvador’s prisons and school boards without mentioning the elections, then little more than three weeks away.

Wallnau, an early evangelical supporter of Donald Trump and co-author of a book promoting Christian control over major social institutions, told followers that they had done their part and could address the election results afterward. Behind closed doors, according to the Guardian, he acknowledged difficulty attracting young people and urged supporters to cultivate leaders who could outlast Trump.

The reporting does not establish that Wallnau has abandoned Trump or the MAGA project. It shows something more calculated: an influential organizer lowering expectations, insulating himself from a possible Republican setback and preparing the movement for succession.

Power is the project

Wallnau is not merely a preacher with changing interests. His “Seven Mountain” politics seeks control over government, media, education and business. The relevant institution here is therefore not a church retreat but an organized political network trained to treat social authority as territory to capture.

His praise for El Salvador’s prison system and favorable attention to countries that have experienced hard-right political surges clarify what kind of power interests him. The Guardian’s account depicts a movement studying concentrated authority abroad while considering how to preserve its influence at home beyond one president.

Retreat without accountability

Wallnau’s message shifts responsibility at the moment responsibility becomes inconvenient. Followers were recruited into a national political campaign; now, facing the prospect of failure, they are told they cannot be responsible for the whole country and might find a “greater benefit” in diet or lifestyle.

That is not evidence that Wallnau caused any electoral outcome, nor does the article establish his private motive. But the foreseeable function of the rhetoric is plain: victories validate the movement, while defeats become impersonal events that simply happen. The organizer keeps his authority; followers are redirected from political consequences to self-management.

The headline outruns the evidence

“Jumping ship” suggests desertion. The reported conduct supports strategic repositioning instead. Wallnau remains focused on the movement’s future, the selection of leaders and the institutions it wants to influence. Professor André Gagné, who studies Wallnau, interprets the shift as careful navigation of fractures within Trump’s coalition and preparation for whoever comes next.

That distinction matters. Personalizing this story as one evangelical losing faith in Trump obscures the more consequential development: Christian nationalist infrastructure is being designed to survive him. Trump may be the movement’s vehicle, but Wallnau’s reported remarks indicate that the destination was never limited to one politician.

Failure as succession planning

The coalition’s weakness with younger people and Wallnau’s concern about leadership after Trump point to an organizational problem, not an ideological conversion. His answer is not withdrawal from politics. It is succession planning, accompanied by rhetoric that cushions supporters against an unfavorable result.

This is how durable political projects manage setbacks. They detach the cause from the immediate candidate, reinterpret defeat as a temporary stage and preserve the network for another campaign. The story is not chiefly about a prominent backer fleeing a sinking ship. It is about a power broker making sure the machinery can be transferred before the captain leaves.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: Robert Reich issues scorching reality check on Trump's 'incessant lies'
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that former Labor Secretary Robert Reich urged voters to reject Donald Trump and Republican candidates in an election scheduled for the Tuesday referenced in his commentary. Reich argued that Trump’s “incessant” lying, attacks on opponents and the press, scapegoating of minority groups, and personal use of presidential power warranted a decisive vote of no confidence. Reich also said Republicans controlled every branch of the federal government and had subordinated
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that former Labor Secretary Robert Reich urged voters to reject Donald Trump and Republican candidates in an election scheduled for the Tuesday referenced in his commentary. Reich argued that Trump’s “incessant” lying, attacks on opponents and the press, scapegoating of minority groups, and personal use of presidential power warranted a decisive vote of no confidence.

Reich also said Republicans controlled every branch of the federal government and had subordinated the party to Trump. He warned that, without electoral restraint, they would pursue cuts to major social programs and further tax reductions for wealthy people and large corporations. The supplied text gives neither a publication date nor the election result, so it does not establish whether voters delivered the rejection Reich sought.

The power is not rhetorical

Trump is the subject of Reich’s condemnation, but Reich locates the operative power in an alliance: a president commanding a Republican Party that controlled the federal government. That distinction matters. Presidential demagoguery becomes policy only when legislators, officials, donors, and party institutions convert it into appointments, budgets, enforcement priorities, and law.

Calling those Republicans “enablers” is accurate but incomplete. They were not spectators who failed to restrain one man. According to Reich’s account, they possessed institutional authority of their own and chose to place it behind him. Trump supplied the political brand; the party supplied the machinery.

Scapegoats are governing tools

Reich identifies a familiar substitution. Republicans promoted supposed dangers associated with Muslims, Mexican and Latino Americans, transgender Americans, allegedly fraudulent voters, and “globalists,” while neglecting climate change, economic inequality, unregulated artificial intelligence, and a costly, ineffective healthcare system.

This is not merely a dispute over which problems deserve attention. Scapegoating redirects anger away from officials and economic interests capable of shaping public policy and toward groups with less power to defend themselves. It turns political failure into a story about contamination by outsiders. The targets become more visible; the decision-makers become less accountable.

AlterNet oversells the confrontation

The headline promises a “scorching reality check” on Trump’s lies. The text provides something broader and less evidentiary: Reich’s election appeal. He lists patterns of conduct and prospective policy consequences, but he does not examine particular false statements or demonstrate, claim by claim, how they collide with reality.

That framing reduces an argument about organized political power to a verbal clash between Reich and Trump. It is clickable, but politically thin. The important issue is not that a former cabinet secretary produced forceful language. It is that, in Reich’s account, an entire governing party accepted Trumpism because doing so preserved its control and advanced its agenda.

The ballot is leverage, not absolution

Reich puts the immediate burden on voters, urging them to “throw the bums out.” Elections are the public’s most direct instrument for removing officeholders, but voter responsibility does not erase elite agency. Party leaders selected their alliances. Legislators chose which proposals to advance. Officials decided whether power would restrain abuse or facilitate it.

Blaming “the judgment of the American people” alone would therefore reproduce the same misdirection Reich otherwise exposes. Citizens cast ballots within a system shaped by parties, concentrated wealth, media incentives, and officeholders who possess far more capacity than any individual voter to determine what government actually does.

The system rewards the decoy

The larger pattern is a governing coalition using cultural targets to secure authority for material decisions. Fear is directed downward; benefits flow upward; institutional actors describe their choices as obedience to a political movement they helped construct.

That arrangement survives when coverage treats politics as a contest of personalities and insults. Reich’s argument is strongest where it points beyond Trump: cruelty can mobilize a constituency, but institutions make it consequential. The systemic error is to stare at the provocateur while the people holding legislative, administrative, and financial power quietly turn provocation into government.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: Humiliation as Trump defangs elite law firms that cut deals with him
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet, summarizing New York Times reporting, says nine major law firms largely withdrew from prominent voting-rights and election litigation after reaching deals with President Donald Trump’s administration. The firms had faced threatened executive orders targeting federal contracts and security clearances; in exchange for avoiding those sanctions, they pledged nearly $1 billion in free legal work for causes favored by Trump. Paul Weiss, once a major source of legal support for
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet, summarizing New York Times reporting, says nine major law firms largely withdrew from prominent voting-rights and election litigation after reaching deals with President Donald Trump’s administration. The firms had faced threatened executive orders targeting federal contracts and security clearances; in exchange for avoiding those sanctions, they pledged nearly $1 billion in free legal work for causes favored by Trump.

Paul Weiss, once a major source of legal support for voting-rights advocates, was among the firms that retreated. Attorney Norm Eisen said chairman Brad Karp was no longer providing advice as Trump sought to influence the midterm elections. The Times also found that some firms erased references to past voting-rights work, while lawyers at one firm reportedly volunteered in secret.

The retreat spread beyond the firms that signed agreements. John Powers of the Advancement Project said other firms had abandoned administration-related civil-rights and voting-rights work, withdrawn support, or insisted upon anonymity. When the Advancement Project and the NAACP challenged Justice Department election-monitoring tactics, they initially proceeded without a private-firm partner.

The White House held the weapon

This was not a dispute among institutions with comparable power. The president controlled the executive machinery capable of disrupting contracts and security clearances. The firms controlled valuable legal expertise, but they also had clients, revenue, and institutional access to protect.

Trump’s administration supplied the coercive pressure. The firms then made their own decisions about how to answer it. Calling the result a generalized “chilling effect” captures the spread of fear but can obscure the chain of responsibility: the White House threatened punishment, firm leaders accepted terms, and voting-rights organizations lost resources.

Capitulation was a choice

The firms were targets of government pressure, but victimhood does not erase agency. Their leaders could assess the legal risks, challenge the threatened orders, or accept commercial damage. According to the reporting, nine chose agreements that protected their institutions while committing enormous legal capacity to presidential priorities.

The consequences were not confined to bruised professional reputations. Partners reportedly pulled out of cases, demanded concealment, or left public-interest groups searching for workarounds. Lawyers volunteering behind their bosses’ backs suggest that the obstacle was not a shortage of legal talent. It was institutional permission.

Prestige without principle

Elite firms routinely market themselves through celebrated civil-rights cases and pro bono commitments. That branding is cheap when the work carries social prestige and limited commercial danger. The relevant test arrives when powerful officials attach a cost to it.

Scrubbing voting-rights histories from firm websites, as the Times reported some had done, is especially revealing. It does not merely reduce exposure; it turns past principle into a liability to be hidden. Paul Weiss and seven other firms reportedly offered no examples when asked about work opposing the administration. Silence here functions less as neutrality than as evidence of what their leadership no longer wishes to defend publicly.

The burden moves downward

The framing of “humiliation” risks making elite lawyers’ loss of stature the central injury. It is not. The sharper consequence falls on civil-rights organizations, voters, and smaller legal teams forced to confront federal power without the money and staffing that major firms once supplied.

The Times reported that the administration had begun election litigation intended to create confusion about the outcome. Whatever those cases ultimately produce, weakened opposition changes the field before a court rules. Institutional retreat increases the cost of every challenge and leaves fewer organizations able to respond quickly.

Coercion scales through compliance

Authoritarian methods do not require every institution to be directly punished. A few visible threats can teach an entire profession to anticipate retaliation. The reporting indicates that firms untouched by the original deals nevertheless began avoiding sensitive cases. That is how coercive power multiplies: not only through orders issued, but through decisions frightened institutions make in advance.

The larger failure is therefore shared but not equal. The administration wielded state power to pressure legal adversaries. Firm leaders converted that pressure into retreat. The resulting void exposes a brittle system in which rights enforcement depends partly on whether wealthy private institutions find courage compatible with their business model.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: Melania hijacked the Pope’s ceasefire as Catholic support for Trump craters
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Wall Street Journal reporter Alex Ward questioned the White House’s portrayal of Melania Trump as a central negotiator of a ceasefire that enabled hundreds of people to leave Russian-occupied Oleshky in southern Ukraine on Friday. Ward said Pope Leo XIV probably did more to construct the agreement, but acknowledged that he lacked sufficient reporting to determine the first lady’s exact role. Ward argued that Moscow, Kyiv, and the White House each had reasons t
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Wall Street Journal reporter Alex Ward questioned the White House’s portrayal of Melania Trump as a central negotiator of a ceasefire that enabled hundreds of people to leave Russian-occupied Oleshky in southern Ukraine on Friday. Ward said Pope Leo XIV probably did more to construct the agreement, but acknowledged that he lacked sufficient reporting to determine the first lady’s exact role.

Ward argued that Moscow, Kyiv, and the White House each had reasons to amplify Melania Trump’s involvement. He suggested Russia could benefit by flattering President Donald Trump’s family, while repeatedly conceding that the first lady may have done substantive work. The reporting does not establish that she “stole” the ceasefire; it establishes skepticism about an official credit claim.

AlterNet also cites Christopher Hale’s account of Pew polling showing Trump’s approval among American Catholics falling from 39 percent in January 2026 to 30 percent six days before the midterms. Pew did not identify a cause. Hale attributed the decline to Trump’s attack on Iran, but the article supplies no evidence demonstrating that this policy caused the shift.

Credit is a form of power

The institutional power here belongs to governments controlling military operations, negotiators able to secure their consent, and authorities capable of moving civilians out of occupied territory. A first lady may exert influence, but she does not command those institutions merely because the White House places her at the center of its story.

That distinction matters because political credit is not ceremonial. Assigning a humanitarian result to a president’s spouse converts an evacuation into family branding. If Pope Leo’s diplomacy supplied the framework, minimizing that work would allow the White House to absorb another institution’s achievement. But Ward’s suspicions are not proof, and AlterNet’s headline is more certain than its evidence.

Flattery as foreign policy leverage

Ward identifies the sharper political possibility: Russia benefits if Trump interprets praise for his wife as generosity toward his family. That is an inference, not an established account of the negotiations. Still, it describes a recognizable vulnerability whenever statecraft becomes personalized around a ruler’s relatives and sensitivities.

The problem is not whether Melania Trump deserves zero credit or all of it. It is that the public has not been given enough evidence to apportion credit at all. Moscow and Kyiv may each have strategic incentives to validate the White House narrative. The White House has an obvious reputational incentive. Those incentives should prompt scrutiny, not a counterclaim presented as settled fact.

The headline outruns the reporting

AlterNet frames the episode as a hijacking, yet its central witness says he is judging “without too much reporting,” calls Melania Trump’s role possible, and says he does not want to discredit her work. That is not evidence of theft. It is an argument that official claims remain inadequately substantiated.

The article also welds the ceasefire dispute to collapsing Catholic approval without showing that Catholics connected the two. Even the cited polling does not explain the decline. Hale’s attribution to Iran may be a hypothesis worth investigating, but the reporting does not provide issue polling, interviews, or other evidence that would establish causation.

The stronger story is institutional

Trump’s reported decline among Catholics is politically significant because he won that electorate by 12 points in 2024. The cited figures also show a particularly steep fall among white Catholics, from 52 percent to 39 percent after January 2026. Those numbers describe movement; they do not explain it.

The broader pattern is a struggle over who gets to define political reality. The White House can use its platform to elevate a family member’s role. Russia can reinforce that account for strategic reasons. Commentators can then replace one unverified narrative with another and call it accountability. The result is not clarity but competing exercises in attribution, each attached to institutional or partisan incentives.

Personality politics obscures consequence

Hundreds of people reportedly left an occupied Ukrainian city under a ceasefire. That human consequence should be the fixed point of the story. Instead, the coverage turns quickly toward who receives prestige and how that prestige intersects with domestic religious polling.

This is what personalized power does: diplomacy becomes family mythology, foreign governments learn to speak through flattery, and journalism is tempted to answer propaganda with overstatement. The necessary correction is less glamorous and more exacting—identify which institutions negotiated, what each participant actually did, and what evidence supports the credit being claimed. Without that work, the public receives a political branding contest where an account of power should be.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: An eleventh-hour gambit is shaking up the midterms
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet, republishing Grist, reports that the Trump administration released billions of dollars in agricultural aid shortly before the 2026 midterm elections, after federal decisions and policies had worsened financial pressure on farmers and ranchers. The USDA announced $8 billion on October 19 to offset crop-year losses associated with high diesel prices, followed by $57 million for independent meat processors on October 26 and a plan to purchase nearly $500 million in American
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet, republishing Grist, reports that the Trump administration released billions of dollars in agricultural aid shortly before the 2026 midterm elections, after federal decisions and policies had worsened financial pressure on farmers and ranchers. The USDA announced $8 billion on October 19 to offset crop-year losses associated with high diesel prices, followed by $57 million for independent meat processors on October 26 and a plan to purchase nearly $500 million in American agricultural commodities.

The reporting says farmers had already endured program rollbacks, rising debt, a six-year high in farm bankruptcies, uncertainty over federal support and the removal of solar from a renewable-energy grant program. Ranchers faced record beef prices, drought-depleted herds and imports they said undercut their businesses. USDA had not yet explained precisely how the $8 billion would be distributed, saying payments were still being determined.

The government created the emergency

The administration holds the relevant institutional power. It controls USDA implementation, shaped the programs that were cut and directed the foreign and energy policies implicated in producers’ rising costs.

A Democratic-led congressional report estimated that disruptions associated with Trump’s war in Iran put farmers on track to spend an additional $2.4 billion on diesel. The administration’s response was not to acknowledge that causal chain. It offered $8 billion in relief and called Trump “the most pro-farmer president” in American history.

That is political messaging substituting for an account of responsibility. The government is presenting itself as the rescuer from conditions its own decisions helped produce.

Relief without repair

Emergency payments may keep farms operating, and their practical value should not be dismissed. But compensation is not the same as correction.

USDA simultaneously made it harder for farmers to reduce their exposure to fuel and utility costs by excluding solar from a popular renewable-energy grant program. The administration is therefore subsidizing losses tied to diesel dependence while narrowing access to one alternative. It pays producers after the damage while preserving the policy structure that leaves them vulnerable to the next shock.

Aaron Lehman of the Iowa Farmers Union supplied the essential distinction: farmers needed help, but “never should have been put in this position.” The payments address immediate pain without resolving who imposed or intensified it.

The election calendar is part of the policy

The timing does not prove an unlawful or explicitly electoral motive, and the reporting does not establish one. It does show an administration suddenly mobilizing large sums as a historically supportive constituency becomes openly dissatisfied and Election Day approaches.

That sequence matters. Farmers waited through months of strain and unclear policy, then received a cascade of announcements in the closing weeks of the campaign. The power on display is not merely the ability to spend federal money. It is the ability to decide when relief becomes available—and then convert that relief into evidence of presidential benevolence.

Calling this an “eleventh-hour gambit” should not obscure the actors. Farmers did not manufacture the crisis to extract a bailout. Federal officials made consequential choices, delayed an adequate response and now control the remedy.

Congress left the structure to rot

The deeper failure extends beyond USDA. The last farm bill was enacted in 2018, while competing replacements remained stalled in the House and Senate at the time of the reporting. A legislative system once expected to renew agricultural policy every five years has left crop insurance, conservation and other central programs subject to prolonged uncertainty.

That vacuum rewards executive improvisation. Instead of durable rules debated and enacted through Congress, producers get administrative reversals, emergency announcements and incomplete implementation details. Institutional paralysis turns public policy into discretionary crisis management—and discretionary crisis management is exceptionally easy to stage as generosity.

Dependency as political leverage

This story reveals a familiar governing pattern: weaken stable support, preserve the sources of vulnerability, then advertise emergency relief as proof of loyalty to the people absorbing the damage.

The misdirection lies in treating rural frustration as a political mood the administration must “smooth over,” rather than a response to identifiable decisions. Farmers and ranchers have agency, but they do not control USDA funding, war policy, federal energy priorities or the congressional calendar. Washington does.

A government that substitutes last-minute payouts for coherent agricultural policy is not solving the underlying problem. It is making insecurity permanent and assistance conditional on the timetable of those in power.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: A perilous 60-day window has DC on high alert
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet describes the roughly 60 days between the November 3, 2026 election and the seating of the new Congress on January 1, 2027 as perilous because Donald Trump would remain president while Democrats might be preparing to take control of Congress. The article reports that Democrats expect Trump to allege election fraud and have prepared lawsuits, enlisted state and local officials, and planned an extensive presence at polling places to defend certified results. The article also
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet describes the roughly 60 days between the November 3, 2026 election and the seating of the new Congress on January 1, 2027 as perilous because Donald Trump would remain president while Democrats might be preparing to take control of Congress. The article reports that Democrats expect Trump to allege election fraud and have prepared lawsuits, enlisted state and local officials, and planned an extensive presence at polling places to defend certified results.

The article also reports federal scrutiny of election matters, including Justice Department subpoenas for California records and an investigation connected to Alaska’s Senate race, alongside plans for 1,000 federal poll monitors. It offers no evidence that the administration had decided to seize ballots, arrest election officials, declare martial law, or obstruct certification; those are scenarios the writer raises, not reported plans.

Its larger argument is that election interference may be less dangerous than events beyond the election itself. Citing Senator Chris Murphy’s account of a classified briefing, the article says the administration was considering a post-midterm escalation against Iran. It then connects that prospect to wider war, energy shocks, support for Russia, technological rivalry with China, and an economy increasingly dependent on artificial-intelligence investment.

The power is already in office

The story’s central imbalance is simple: Democrats may have lawyers, observers and prospective congressional majorities, but the president controls the executive branch until his term ends. The Justice Department, Department of Homeland Security and FBI possess coercive authority that election watchdogs do not. A stack of prepared lawsuits is a defense against government action, not an equal share of government power.

That distinction matters because the article sometimes treats universal expectation as reassurance. Officials anticipating an abuse does not prevent it. Courts can reject unlawful claims, but litigation operates after somebody with institutional power has initiated the confrontation. Preparation can limit damage; it cannot make the power imbalance disappear.

Speculation is not evidence

The article is strongest when it identifies reported actions and weakest when it races ahead of them. Subpoenas, investigations and planned federal monitoring deserve scrutiny, especially if officials use unsupported fraud claims to justify them. But the article does not establish that federal agents were ordered to intimidate voters or that Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson had agreed to obstruct certification.

The same evidentiary problem infects its international claims. Murphy’s warning about an undisclosed plan is properly attributed, but the article then declares potential attacks on Iranian energy infrastructure to be war crimes without supplying the legal or operational facts needed to sustain that conclusion. Its allegations that Trump, Vladimir Putin and Elon Musk conspired to sabotage Ukraine, and that China bribed Trump to conceal a spy, are presented without enough supporting detail in the supplied text to treat them as established facts.

That is not rigor. It is an argument outrunning its evidence—and therefore making serious, supportable concerns easier to dismiss.

The constitutional guardrail is political

AlterNet places considerable faith in the constitutional allocation of election administration to states and localities. That allocation is real within the article’s account, but constitutional text does not enforce itself. Election officials must resist pressure, judges must issue and enforce rulings, executive officers must obey them, and Congress must perform its assigned role.

The article’s language obscures this agency when it says “the bones of the republic” will probably hold. Institutions are not bones. They are people making decisions under incentives and pressure. If officials enable unlawful conduct, institutional failure is their act—not an unfortunate structural collapse without authors.

Crisis is an instrument

The article’s most useful insight is that the election may not be the only arena in which concentrated executive power matters. A military escalation could produce consequences faster than election litigation can contain them. Murphy’s reported warning points toward a decision made behind classification barriers, with Congress and the public left to confront the results after the machinery is moving.

War, fuel-price shocks and economic instability can also reorder domestic politics. They create fear, expand demands for executive action and divert attention from accountability. The reporting does not establish that such disruption is being deliberately engineered for political advantage. But it does identify the conditions under which officials can convert an external crisis into additional domestic leverage.

The system rewards the first mover

The larger pattern is not simply an unstable president facing a tense transition. It is a political system that gives the incumbent enormous capacity to act while assigning everyone else the slower work of challenging, reviewing and repairing those actions.

AlterNet is right to focus on who can move first, but its overheated allegations weaken that analysis. The danger disclosed by its better-supported reporting is concrete enough: executive agencies can launch investigations, deploy personnel and escalate military operations before courts, Congress or voters can impose consequences. A system dependent on retrospective correction repeatedly gives power the initiative—and makes accountability arrive late, if it arrives at all.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.
