item.title: Newsmax host visibly cringes as Boebert gets smacked around in debate
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Democratic challenger Eileen Laubacher confronted Republican Representative Lauren Boebert during a recent debate over the reported Iran war, arguing that Boebert should vote against it if she believed war was never justified. Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral, delivered the remark after Boebert interrupted her and accused her of previously agreeing that war was good for business. Newsmax host Greg Kelly later played the exchange while interviewing Boeber
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Democratic challenger Eileen Laubacher confronted Republican Representative Lauren Boebert during a recent debate over the reported Iran war, arguing that Boebert should vote against it if she believed war was never justified. Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral, delivered the remark after Boebert interrupted her and accused her of previously agreeing that war was good for business.

Newsmax host Greg Kelly later played the exchange while interviewing Boebert. His tightened expression and hesitant response are the basis for AlterNet’s claim that he “cringed,” though he did not say Boebert had performed badly. When invited to explain Laubacher, Boebert called her a “Deep State candidate” and alleged that she held millions of dollars in defense stocks, owned multiple homes, and had misrepresented her views on war. The article provides no independent substantiation or response from Laubacher to those claims.

Kelly then suggested that some veterans had been “weaponized by the deep state” and were using military service “as a weapon.” He ended the interview shortly afterward by wishing Boebert luck.

The incumbent holds the power

The consequential fact is not that Boebert endured an awkward television segment. It is that she is a sitting member of Congress confronting a challenger who asked how she would use the power she already possesses.

Laubacher’s argument was direct: if Boebert opposes the Iran war under discussion, she should vote against it. Boebert did not answer that challenge in the exchange AlterNet describes. She redirected the debate toward disputed remarks by her opponent and, later, toward her wealth, investments, property and supposed association with the “deep state.”

That distinction matters. Laubacher can criticize military policy. Boebert can cast congressional votes. Treating their disagreement primarily as a campaign spectacle obscures who currently has institutional agency.

Accusation replaced accountability

Boebert’s response followed a familiar political maneuver: when pressed about an exercise of public power, put the questioner on trial instead. The resulting pile of accusations was expansive enough to crowd out the original issue but, in AlterNet’s account, insufficiently documented to resolve any of it.

Potential conflicts involving defense investments would be legitimate subjects for scrutiny if established with records and presented with Laubacher’s response. “Deep state,” however, supplies no comparable evidence. It converts an opponent’s government and military background into proof of hidden disloyalty without identifying an institution, decision or act for which she can be held accountable.

The purpose of that rhetoric, whatever Boebert’s private motive, is clear in practice: it replaces a testable question about an incumbent’s vote with an insinuation that the challenger belongs to a shadowy enemy network.

Newsmax supplied the escape route

Kelly briefly appeared uncertain after showing the debate clip, but his next move was not to press Boebert on the vote Laubacher had raised. He asked what constituents “need to know” about her opponent. That invitation allowed Boebert to leave her own record behind and resume attacking Laubacher.

Kelly then strengthened the diversion by suggesting that veterans can be “weaponized by the deep state.” This was not neutral moderation. It gave conspiratorial language a television host’s endorsement and recast Laubacher’s military experience as presumptively suspect precisely when that experience supported her challenge on war.

The segment therefore exposed more than a strained reaction shot. It showed an allied media figure recognizing an uncomfortable exchange, then helping the incumbent change the subject.

The spectacle conceals the decision

AlterNet’s framing is weakest where it fixates on who “smacked around” whom. Debate humiliation is campaign entertainment. War policy is the exercise of state power, with consequences far beyond either candidate’s performance.

The article also appends allegations and scandals involving Boebert and her family that do not establish what she would do about the conflict. That material may intensify the portrait of a vulnerable incumbent, but it repeats the same structural error as the interview: personality and scandal displace the decision that only the officeholder can make.

The larger pattern is political evasion reinforced by partisan media. An incumbent is asked to account for her authority; she attacks the challenger’s identity and finances; the host validates the attack; and coverage packages the episode as embarrassment. The supposed cringe is incidental. The real story is how quickly responsibility for government action disappeared from view.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: The booming stock market is masking a deeper American financial crisis
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that the booming stock market and strong headline indicators are concealing widespread economic strain. Political scientist Erin Kay Lockwood argues that consumer spending, business investment, low unemployment and GDP growth do not capture how unevenly prosperity is distributed—or why consumer sentiment in 2026 remained 10% below its level a year earlier. Inflation fell from 9.1% in June 2022 to 3.7% in September 2026, yet sentiment was lower than at the inflation
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that the booming stock market and strong headline indicators are concealing widespread economic strain. Political scientist Erin Kay Lockwood argues that consumer spending, business investment, low unemployment and GDP growth do not capture how unevenly prosperity is distributed—or why consumer sentiment in 2026 remained 10% below its level a year earlier.

Inflation fell from 9.1% in June 2022 to 3.7% in September 2026, yet sentiment was lower than at the inflation peak. Inflation-adjusted wages rose between 2022 and the first half of 2026 before beginning to fall, while the richest 10% of Americans generated half of consumer spending and spending by the bottom 80% failed to keep pace with inflation.

That divide carries immediate political consequences. An October 2026 Pew Research survey found that 84% of registered voters considered the economy very important to their midterm vote. AlterNet reports that Republicans faced grim polling ahead of the November 3 election and that Democrats were expected to gain substantially, although those projections did not establish the election’s outcome.

The averages serve the winners

The apparent contradiction disappears once the economy is treated as a distribution of power rather than a national average. If affluent households can sustain aggregate spending while most earners lose purchasing power, “strong consumer spending” describes the volume of transactions without identifying who can afford them.

The stock market creates the same distortion. The top 0.1% of households hold five times as much wealth as the bottom half of the country. Rising asset prices therefore register as broad economic strength while delivering their largest gains to a narrow ownership class. The metric is accurate. The political use of it is misleading.

Power sits above the consumer

Ordinary households do not set tariff policy, determine the tax treatment of wealth or decide whether economic management will prioritize asset values over purchasing power. Those choices belong to elected officials and institutions with authority over trade, taxation and monetary policy.

In 2026, President Donald Trump and a Republican-controlled Congress held the most immediate electoral responsibility for federal economic policy. But the inequality described in the reporting grew over roughly two decades, narrowing briefly during the crises of 2008 and 2020 before widening again. That record implicates a durable governing structure, not a single election cycle.

“Vibes” is an evasion

Calling public pessimism “vibes” shifts scrutiny from economic arrangements to the supposed irrationality of the people living under them. The reporting supplies a more concrete explanation: falling real wages in recent months, spending that has failed to match inflation for the bottom 80%, and wealth gains concentrated among households that already own most financial assets.

Consumer sentiment may also reflect judgments about the country as a whole, not merely respondents’ personal finances. That is not confusion. Voters can recognize that an economy is producing impressive totals while distributing security, ownership and opportunity upward.

The ballot assigns responsibility

The governing party possesses the institutional power and therefore bears the immediate political exposure. If voters punish Republicans in the 2026 midterms, that would not prove any single economic theory, but it would show the limits of campaigning on aggregate growth while household insecurity remains widespread.

Democrats gaining seats would not itself repair the structure. Electoral backlash can change who administers an unequal economy without changing who benefits from it. The consequential question is whether lawmakers alter the distribution of income, wealth and risk—or simply wait for improving sentiment to rescue the same policies.

The crisis is political measurement

The deeper failure is not that conventional indicators are false. It is that officials routinely present them as sufficient. Aggregate growth can coexist with shrinking purchasing power for most earners; record markets can coexist with extreme wealth concentration; low unemployment can coexist with profound insecurity.

That framing protects the institutions and asset owners doing well under the current arrangement. It converts distributional conflict into a communications problem and material hardship into public misunderstanding. The system is not failing to produce wealth. It is producing wealth, concentrating it, and then citing the total as evidence that everyone else should feel better.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: The Medieval loophole that lets Donald Trump say whatever he wants
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Donald Trump called Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed a “jihadist” and a member of the Muslim Brotherhood during a midterm campaign. The article says no evidence supported those labels and argues that sovereign immunity could prevent El-Sayed from pursuing a defamation claim against Trump. Under the process described, the Justice Department can certify that a federal official acted within the scope of employment. The United States then replac
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Donald Trump called Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed a “jihadist” and a member of the Muslim Brotherhood during a midterm campaign. The article says no evidence supported those labels and argues that sovereign immunity could prevent El-Sayed from pursuing a defamation claim against Trump.

Under the process described, the Justice Department can certify that a federal official acted within the scope of employment. The United States then replaces that official as the defendant, and because Congress has not waived federal immunity for defamation claims, the court dismisses the case for lack of jurisdiction.

The Supreme Court has not decided whether presidents and members of Congress count as federal employees for this purpose. AlterNet notes, however, that federal appellate courts have protected legislators, while one circuit has extended that protection to the president.

Power without exposure

The institutional advantage belongs to federal officeholders and the executive branch. A candidate targeted by a damaging accusation must bear its political consequences immediately. The official who made it may receive a government-funded route out of court before any judge evaluates whether the statement was false or defamatory.

That distinction matters. Sovereign immunity does not establish that Trump’s statements were lawful, accurate, or harmless. It can prevent adjudication altogether. The doctrine converts public office from the source of responsibility into a possible shield against it.

The government closes the courthouse

This outcome is not produced by medieval history acting on its own. Congress retained immunity for defamation when it authorized other claims against the federal government. Courts then interpreted the protection broadly, including rulings that legislators’ social-media posts can fall within their official duties.

The Justice Department supplies the crucial procedural trigger by certifying that the speaker acted within the scope of federal employment. That gives the executive branch power to help transform an individual official’s alleged reputational attack into a claim against an immune sovereign.

Trump did not create this structure. But, as AlterNet presents the episode, he could benefit from a system maintained by Congress, administered by the Justice Department, and enlarged through judicial interpretation.

The weaker actor is not the loophole

Coverage of inflammatory political speech often drifts toward the target’s reaction, the campaign controversy, or the difficulty of proving reputational damage. That framing misplaces agency. El-Sayed did not create the legal asymmetry; federal institutions did.

Nor should an unsupported allegation be softened into mere campaign “rhetoric.” According to AlterNet, Trump attached terrorism-associated labels to a Muslim candidate without evidence. Whatever his unproven intent, the foreseeable political effect was to invite voters to view El-Sayed through suspicion and fear rather than his record or platform.

The legal system described here compounds that imbalance: the powerful speaker receives institutional protection, while the target carries the burden of an accusation the courts may never examine.

Immunity becomes political infrastructure

Defamation law ordinarily distinguishes protected opinion from actionable false statements through litigation. Sovereign immunity can block that inquiry before it begins. The resulting privilege is especially consequential during elections, when a false allegation can circulate quickly and corrective information may arrive after voters have acted.

This is not simply an archaic phrase surviving from English common law. It is operational infrastructure. A doctrine associated with the claim that “the king can do no wrong” persists because modern institutions continue to preserve and apply it.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is a familiar inversion of democratic accountability: public power expands the official’s reach while narrowing the injured person’s remedy. The government speaker can use the authority and visibility of office to shape an election, then invoke that same governmental status as protection from ordinary legal scrutiny.

AlterNet’s account does not establish that every presidential statement is immune, and the Supreme Court has left the central classification question unresolved. It establishes something narrower and still corrosive: existing appellate precedent and federal procedure may deny a targeted citizen even the chance to test a defamation claim.

A republic does not need a literal monarch to reproduce monarchical privilege. It needs only institutions willing to preserve exceptional protection for the people already holding exceptional power.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: A damning new report targeting Trump is being met with near-total silence
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that House Judiciary Committee Democrats released a 53-page report on Monday alleging that Donald Trump participated in sexual abuse connected to Jeffrey Epstein and that the Justice Department and FBI have withheld relevant evidence. The committee called for a special counsel. Trump has not been charged or convicted on the allegations described in the article. The report compiles accounts from 11 women, largely drawn from public records and documents released unde
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that House Judiciary Committee Democrats released a 53-page report on Monday alleging that Donald Trump participated in sexual abuse connected to Jeffrey Epstein and that the Justice Department and FBI have withheld relevant evidence. The committee called for a special counsel. Trump has not been charged or convicted on the allegations described in the article.

The report compiles accounts from 11 women, largely drawn from public records and documents released under the Epstein Files Transparency Act. According to Miami Herald reporter Julie K. Brown, its principal new disclosure is Beatrice Keul’s allegation that Trump raped her at New York’s Plaza Hotel in November 1993 after Epstein arranged their meeting. AlterNet’s central claim is that major newspapers and cable networks largely ignored the report; the article cites a media-monitoring comparison showing only two cable-news mentions of the rape allegation during a period in which “cheesecake” received 368.

Power is not evenly distributed

The women making these allegations do not possess subpoena power, prosecutorial authority, control over federal records, or command of a national media platform. Trump holds the presidency. The Justice Department and FBI control evidence and investigative decisions. Congressional committees can investigate and expose, but the House minority cannot compel the executive branch to police itself.

That hierarchy matters. Treating this as merely another dispute between Democrats and Trump would erase the decisive imbalance: one side is asking institutions to investigate allegations against the person who commands the executive branch; the other side controls those institutions.

The decisions behind the silence

House Judiciary Democrats chose to assemble the accounts, publish the report, and request a special counsel. Federal law-enforcement officials, according to the committee, have kept significant material redacted. That is the committee’s allegation, not an independently established finding in AlterNet’s article, but it identifies the officials whose conduct requires scrutiny.

Editors and television producers also exercise power. Near-total silence is not an atmospheric condition. It is the cumulative result of decisions about assignments, airtime, placement, and repetition. AlterNet’s comparison does not prove why those decisions were made, but it does document a grotesque disparity in attention.

Electoral relevance is the wrong test

AlterNet argues that the press discounted the report because it was unlikely to change the approaching midterm election. That motive is the author’s interpretation, not something established by quoted newsroom officials. The observed failure is still plain: serious, attributed allegations against a sitting president received little coverage despite a congressional report and a newly public accuser.

The electoral scoreboard turns accountability into campaign trivia. Under that logic, alleged crimes matter chiefly when they can move polling numbers. Once reporters decide an allegation will not alter an election, the people alleging harm become politically disposable and institutional conduct escapes sustained examination.

Allegations require scrutiny, not erasure

The committee’s language is more conclusive than the evidence presented in AlterNet’s article permits an outside reader to adopt. These are grave allegations, and the report’s claim that they satisfy the FBI threshold for opening an investigation is not the same as proof beyond a reasonable doubt, a criminal charge, or a conviction. Precision protects the accusers as much as the accused: sensational overstatement gives powerful subjects an easy excuse to dismiss the entire record.

But uncertainty is a reason to investigate, not a license to look away. Responsible coverage would identify what is newly alleged, what documentation supports each account, what Trump or his representatives deny, what evidence remains redacted, and why federal authorities have or have not acted. Silence performs none of those tasks.

Impunity is built institution by institution

This story is not only about one congressional report. It is about how concentrated power survives serious accusations: executive agencies control the files, legislators divide accountability along party lines, and major news organizations decide that attention depends on immediate electoral payoff.

No single omission establishes a coordinated cover-up. Together, however, institutional passivity produces a predictable consequence. Alleged victims struggle to be heard, officials avoid explaining their choices, and the most powerful person in the system receives the benefit of public exhaustion. Impunity rarely requires everyone to conspire. It often requires only that each institution find its own respectable reason to do nothing.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: The major Trump bombs waiting to detonate right after Election Day
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that several Trump administration actions may have been delayed until after Election Day, including a possible expansion of military conflict with Iran, new abortion restrictions, intensified immigration enforcement and further cuts to health insurance coverage. The article does not establish that each action will occur; it describes preparations, reported plans and anticipated policy moves. According to AlterNet, the Pentagon was ordered to send another aircraft c
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that several Trump administration actions may have been delayed until after Election Day, including a possible expansion of military conflict with Iran, new abortion restrictions, intensified immigration enforcement and further cuts to health insurance coverage. The article does not establish that each action will occur; it describes preparations, reported plans and anticipated policy moves.

According to AlterNet, the Pentagon was ordered to send another aircraft carrier group to the Middle East, while diplomatic personnel and their families were warned to evacuate because of possible retaliation. The administration was also described as pursuing legal challenges over voting while political coverage focused heavily on prospective congressional leadership fights and the 2028 presidential field.

The power is still in the White House

Election forecasts do not command aircraft carriers, direct federal agents or determine how executive agencies enforce federal policy. The presidency does. Even if voters strip Trump’s party of congressional power, the administration retains enormous authority until the next Congress is seated—and some actions can create consequences that no later hearing or investigation can readily reverse.

That is the central political fact obscured by premature discussion of who might lead a Democratic majority. Hakeem Jeffries, Chuck Schumer, Mike Johnson and Jim Jordan matter, but none of those personnel contests answers the immediate question: what will the executive branch do with the power it still possesses?

Preparation is a decision

The article cannot establish that Trump will order new attacks on Iran. It does, however, report concrete military and diplomatic preparations for that possibility. Moving a carrier group and warning diplomatic families to evacuate are institutional acts, not campaign chatter.

Preparation does not make war inevitable, but it narrows the distance between presidential impulse and military action. It also shifts personnel, money and risk before Congress has settled whether it will authorize or fund an expanded conflict. AlterNet reports that Trump rejects congressional involvement in approving or defunding such efforts. That places the constitutional dispute where it belongs: between an executive claiming broad latitude and a legislature whose war and spending powers are meaningful only if lawmakers use them.

Speculation becomes camouflage

Coverage of leadership rivalries offers familiar characters, clean narratives and little immediate accountability. Speculating about Jordan’s ambitions or the cohesion of a future Democratic caucus is easier than tracking delayed regulations, agency directives, troop movements and election litigation.

That emphasis misdirects attention from actors exercising power toward politicians who may acquire it later. It also turns deliberate government choices into atmospheric “troubles,” as though policies simply descend after Election Day. Administrations do not accidentally restrict abortion access, intensify immigration enforcement or reduce health coverage. Officials develop, approve and execute those policies. Where AlterNet identifies only reported or anticipated plans, certainty would be unwarranted—but scrutiny is not.

Elections do not suspend consequences

A decisive result would not instantly transfer authority. AlterNet notes that some counts could take weeks and anticipates litigation and certification fights before winners take office in January. During that interval, the existing administration remains capable of acting at home and abroad.

The consequences are not abstract. Military escalation could expose service members, diplomats and civilians to retaliation without any assurance of achieving the stated goals. Restrictions on abortion travel or medication would fall most heavily on people with the least money and mobility. Immigration campaigns and health-coverage cuts would be administered through federal institutions whose coercive power does not diminish because an election has occurred.

The lame-duck illusion

American political coverage often treats Election Day as the end of one government and the immediate beginning of another. Institutionally, it is neither. Power persists through counting, litigation, certification and the seating of successors.

That gap is not dead time. It is a period in which departing or politically weakened officials may still impose durable costs while journalists inventory the winners’ ambitions. The larger pattern is a press drawn to personalities just as executive power becomes most consequential. The question after an election is not merely who won. It is who can still act, who enabled those actions and who will bear the damage before the new balance of power becomes real.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

← Back to all stories

item.title: Trump performs creepy pantomime of US ally's 'beautiful' president
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Donald Trump used a South Carolina rally to reenact an alleged conversation with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum about his renaming of the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America.” Trump portrayed Sheinbaum pleading with him to reverse the change, then said that “everybody’s happy.” The report provides no confirmation from Sheinbaum that this exchange occurred as Trump described it. During the performance, Trump repeatedly commented on Sheinbaum’s beauty an
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Donald Trump used a South Carolina rally to reenact an alleged conversation with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum about his renaming of the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America.” Trump portrayed Sheinbaum pleading with him to reverse the change, then said that “everybody’s happy.” The report provides no confirmation from Sheinbaum that this exchange occurred as Trump described it.

During the performance, Trump repeatedly commented on Sheinbaum’s beauty and voice while claiming politicians are no longer permitted to call women beautiful. AlterNet notes that he has made similar remarks before, including about Sheinbaum and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.

Trump also misstated the relative ages of Mexico and the United States and understated how long the Gulf of Mexico has carried its established name. The rally was interrupted by two protesters, while a planned Kansas appearance was reportedly canceled; the article cites speculation about protests and polling but does not establish why the cancellation occurred.

Power disguised as grievance

The person exercising power here was not Sheinbaum, the protesters, or some imaginary censor policing compliments. It was the president of the United States, publicly celebrating his government’s decision to impose a new American name on a geographic feature shared with Mexico and Cuba.

Trump nevertheless cast himself as the constrained party. He complained that social rules supposedly prevent him from discussing a woman’s appearance, even as he did exactly that before a rally audience. This is manufactured victimhood: wield institutional authority, then redirect attention toward a trivial restriction that did not restrict him.

A counterpart reduced to a performance

Trump’s pantomime assigned every role in advance. He was decisive; Sheinbaum was pleading. He acted; she reacted. Because AlterNet offers no independent confirmation of the conversation, the reenactment establishes only how Trump chose to portray a neighboring country’s president.

The fixation on Sheinbaum’s appearance further diminished her institutional position. She is Mexico’s head of government, yet Trump presented her as a flattering voice attached to an anxious supplicant. That is not diplomatic analysis. It is a gendered display of hierarchy performed for domestic political consumption.

The renaming is the substance

The article’s “creepy” framing captures the personal conduct but risks making the spectacle seem like the whole story. The consequential act was the assertion of unilateral naming power: the United States changing its official terminology and Trump presenting Mexico’s objection as helpless protest.

His factual errors served that performance. Mexico is not 150 years older than the United States, and AlterNet reports that the Gulf of Mexico has carried its name since 1550. The inaccuracies matter because they strip history down to whatever makes domination sound natural. The message was not that Trump had mastered the past. It was that facts were subordinate to his declaration.

Protest is not an explanation

The story’s closing turn toward disrupted rallies and the canceled Kansas event is less secure. AlterNet reports two protesters in South Carolina and says the Kansas cancellation followed vocal protests at Trump’s previous appearance there. It also cites commentators who suspected polling played a role.

Those facts do not establish why the event was canceled. Treating speculation as an answer would reproduce the same problem visible in Trump’s alleged conversation: a politically useful narrative filling the space where verified evidence should be.

The politics of invented helplessness

The larger pattern is power presenting itself as persecution. Trump described a foreign leader as pleading, an old geographic name as disposable, and himself as endangered by etiquette while he controlled the stage, the story, and the federal naming decision.

That inversion is politically useful. It converts domination into defiance and accountability into censorship. The spectacle invites the audience to focus on whether the performance was strange or offensive. The systemic error is deeper: an officeholder used state power, historical fabrication, and a caricature of an allied president to make unilateralism look like victory—and grievance look like courage.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: Darline Graham pal says she's faking who she really is
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that former South Carolina state Sen. Katrina Shealy, a Republican, accused her longtime friend Darline Graham of presenting a campaign persona that does not reflect the woman Shealy knows. Five days before the election, Shealy told CNN she believed Graham was following direction from Donald Trump’s campaign while running for the Senate seat previously held by her late brother, Lindsey Graham. Shealy endorsed Democrat Annie Andrews instead, calling Andrews authenti
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that former South Carolina state Sen. Katrina Shealy, a Republican, accused her longtime friend Darline Graham of presenting a campaign persona that does not reflect the woman Shealy knows. Five days before the election, Shealy told CNN she believed Graham was following direction from Donald Trump’s campaign while running for the Senate seat previously held by her late brother, Lindsey Graham.

Shealy endorsed Democrat Annie Andrews instead, calling Andrews authentic and more attentive to South Carolinians harmed by higher grocery and gas prices and by failures in social services and juvenile justice. Shealy did not offer specific examples of Graham privately contradicting her campaign positions, and she conceded that Graham might genuinely feel as strongly about Trump as she publicly suggests.

Shealy said she had known Graham through South Carolina politics, including Graham’s appointment to lead the state Commission for the Blind. Asked whether Graham was qualified, Shealy expressed hope that Graham would govern according to her own judgment rather than outside orders.

The endorsement economy

The central issue is not whether Graham is secretly nicer, more moderate or more independent than her campaign suggests. Voters cannot elect a private personality. They elect the candidate who seeks power, accepts political obligations and announces how she intends to use the office.

Shealy’s account describes an endorsement as a transaction: Trump supplies political credibility, and Graham adapts herself to the coalition granting it. That does not prove Graham is being controlled. It does identify the structure of the bargain. A candidate who treats another politician’s approval as something requiring her to “play the game” is surrendering autonomy before acquiring institutional power.

Agency cannot be outsourced

CNN’s Boris Sanchez framed Graham as possibly having been “led astray.” That language shifts responsibility from the candidate making choices to the political force influencing her. Shealy used similar language when she said Graham was being “swayed” and listening to “the wrong side.”

Influence is not coercion. On the evidence presented, Graham chose the endorsement and the campaign posture accompanying it. Unless reporting establishes threats, deception or some other constraint, she remains responsible for what she says and for the alliances she uses to win office. Portraying a candidate as merely misled turns strategic compliance into personal confusion.

Friendship is not evidence

Shealy’s history with Graham gives her testimony political significance, but it does not give her access to Graham’s “heart.” Her strongest claim—that Graham does not believe what she is saying—is also the claim least supported by concrete evidence in AlterNet’s account.

The article’s provocative premise therefore outruns its reporting. It establishes that a former Republican senator who knows Graham distrusts her campaign presentation and supports her Democratic opponent. It does not establish that Graham is faking her beliefs. Shealy herself leaves open the possibility that Graham’s public allegiance is sincere.

That uncertainty matters. The defensible criticism is not that Graham has concealed an authentic self. It is that the candidate’s stated positions, political patrons and willingness to follow them are the available evidence voters must judge.

Who bears the consequences

Shealy’s most substantive point concerns the distance between political decision-makers and people living with the consequences of government choices. She argued that rising grocery and gas costs fall hardest on residents without legislators’ financial protection, including people caught in strained social-service and juvenile-justice systems.

Yet the reporting provides no specific policy comparison showing what either candidate would do about those conditions. “Authenticity” becomes a substitute for examining budgets, votes and administrative power. Character may influence governing, but institutions distribute food assistance, oversee juvenile confinement and fund public services. Sentiment does not.

The larger error

This story reveals a familiar political evasion: campaigns become arguments about who a candidate “really is” while the machinery of power remains underexamined. Endorsers, party networks and campaign organizations matter because they shape access to office and the obligations carried into it—not because they corrupt an otherwise pure inner self.

The relevant question is simpler and harsher. What is Graham willing to say, whom is she willing to follow, and what power would those choices place behind? Whatever she privately believes, the public version is the one asking to govern.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: Federal judge deals Trump admin major blow over Medicaid restrictions
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened A federal judge in Boston blocked one part of the Trump administration’s Medicaid work-requirement rule, finding that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services used an unlawful definition of “medically frail.” AlterNet reports that Judge Richard Stearns ruled for the District of Columbia and a 25-state coalition because CMS went beyond what Congress authorized in the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The decision prevents that definition from being used to disenroll otherwise eli
item.content:encoded:
What happened

A federal judge in Boston blocked one part of the Trump administration’s Medicaid work-requirement rule, finding that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services used an unlawful definition of “medically frail.” AlterNet reports that Judge Richard Stearns ruled for the District of Columbia and a 25-state coalition because CMS went beyond what Congress authorized in the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

The decision prevents that definition from being used to disenroll otherwise eligible patients and gives states six months of protection from penalties tied to implementation errors or delays. It does not stop the broader requirement that many low-income adults covered through Medicaid expansion work or volunteer 80 hours a month, or attend school at least half-time, beginning in January.

Stearns upheld other restrictions, including CMS’s 12-month limit on older medical records used to establish frailty and its policy allowing states to reject self-attestation. Eight states reportedly plan to require medical documentation in 2027. CMS did not immediately comment, and a separate challenge remains pending in Maryland federal court.

The injury came from policy, not paperwork

The administration did not merely create an administrative inconvenience. CMS adopted a definition that, according to the court, exceeded the statute and risked stripping health coverage from chronically ill people who remained legally eligible.

That distinction matters. The vulnerable patients were not the decision-makers, and their illnesses were not the institutional problem. Federal officials wrote the restriction. States were then expected to construct verification systems around it. Patients would bear the consequences when those systems failed, demanded inaccessible evidence, or classified illness too narrowly.

Calling this a dispute over “implementation” would conceal the chain of responsibility. The machinery is bureaucratic; the choice to impose it is political.

The court corrected only the overreach

Stearns exercised substantial but limited power. He stopped CMS from enforcing one unlawful definition and temporarily protected states from penalties while they prepared their systems. He did not dismantle the work requirement Congress enacted or invalidate the administration’s remaining rules.

That makes “major blow” an inflated frame if it suggests the Medicaid restrictions were broadly defeated. The central structure survives. Many recipients must still repeatedly prove work, volunteering, schooling, or eligibility for an exemption to keep health coverage.

The ruling matters because some vulnerable people may avoid wrongful disenrollment. It is not a reversal of the policy that makes continued medical care contingent on navigating a compliance regime.

States can become gatekeepers

The administration’s self-attestation policy gives states discretion during the first year, and eight have already chosen documentation requirements for 2027, citing fraud concerns. The reporting supplies no evidence establishing the scale of that alleged fraud or showing that it outweighs the risk of eligible people losing coverage.

The power imbalance is plain. A state can demand paperwork; a sick person must obtain and submit it. A government can disregard records more than 12 months old; a patient whose condition has not recently required hospitalization must somehow produce fresher proof.

Stearns found CMS had a rational basis for the 12-month lookback period. That legal conclusion does not erase its foreseeable burden. A rule can survive judicial review while still making access harder for the people least equipped to contest an erroneous denial.

Suspicion is the governing premise

Work requirements recast public health insurance as a reward for demonstrated compliance rather than coverage for eligible people. Exemptions do not eliminate that premise. They force those unable to satisfy the work rule to prove, repeatedly and on government-approved terms, that their hardship is legitimate.

Fraud rhetoric reinforces the design by presenting applicants as presumptive cheats and documentation barriers as neutral safeguards. The weaker actor is then blamed for missing a form, lacking a recent record, or failing to navigate a system built by institutions with vastly greater resources.

The larger pattern is governance through attrition. Congress creates the condition, an agency narrows the escape routes, states choose how aggressively to police them, and eligible patients disappear from the rolls through accumulated procedural friction. Courts may block an unlawful component, but the broader political project remains: make survival benefits harder to retain, then describe the resulting losses as individual failures.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: Trump’s increasingly bizarre behavior reaches a tipping point
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Guardian columnist Margaret Sullivan argues Donald Trump’s campaign appearances had become a political liability for Republicans ahead of the following week’s midterm elections. Trump repeatedly urged voters to treat Republican candidates as stand-ins for him, despite his weak approval ratings and public frustration over living costs. Sullivan pointed to Trump’s disjointed remarks, insults, fixation on popularity and unusually personal comments about male poli
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Guardian columnist Margaret Sullivan argues Donald Trump’s campaign appearances had become a political liability for Republicans ahead of the following week’s midterm elections. Trump repeatedly urged voters to treat Republican candidates as stand-ins for him, despite his weak approval ratings and public frustration over living costs.

Sullivan pointed to Trump’s disjointed remarks, insults, fixation on popularity and unusually personal comments about male politicians’ bodies. She also cited conservative Wall Street Journal columnist Jason Riley, who said some MAGA supporters and congressional Republicans had grown tired of Trump’s conduct.

The reporting presents this criticism as a possible turning point, not an established electoral shift. It supplies no polling showing that Trump’s appearances changed votes and no election results proving that Republicans were harmed.

The power is still his

Trump was not merely an eccentric entertainer wandering onto Republican stages. He was the president, the party’s central political figure and the person instructing voters to understand congressional races as a referendum on him. Republican candidates and officials enabled that arrangement by continuing to campaign within a political structure organized around his approval.

That institutional reality matters more than whether his dancing looked awkward or his remarks sounded strange. A president can direct attention, define party loyalty and impose political costs on dissenters. Republican irritation becomes meaningful only when officials use their own power to resist him. The article reports fatigue, not a revolt.

Spectacle obscures the decision

The “bizarre behavior” framing turns a calculated party strategy into a personality story. Trump chose to make himself the subject of elections in which he was not on the ballot. Republican candidates accepted his intervention because his supporters remained valuable to them. Those are political decisions, not symptoms of collective bewilderment.

Cataloguing rambling transitions, childish insults and comments about politicians’ physiques may illustrate his public conduct. But it can also shrink the issue into a question of taste: Is the performance finally too embarrassing? That lets party officials appear trapped by Trump’s personality when they repeatedly treated his prominence as electorally useful.

Allies discover a liability

Right-wing criticism is presented as significant because it came from people who had tolerated or supported Trump. Yet the timing exposes the narrowness of the objection. The reported concern is that his behavior may now hurt Republicans—not that concentrating a party around one leader was inherently corrosive.

This is institutional cowardice dressed as strategic reassessment. As reported, allies began tiring of Trump when his dominance threatened to cost them votes. Their complaint was not that he demanded personal loyalty from an entire party, but that the demand might have stopped paying.

The cost of personalization

Trump’s instruction to imagine him on every ballot erased distinctions among candidates, offices and local consequences. It converted representative elections into a loyalty test centered on one national figure. That strategy could energize committed supporters, as Sullivan acknowledged, while also mobilizing voters who opposed him.

The larger pattern is a party surrendering its identity to a leader and then treating his declining usefulness as an unexpected crisis. The spectacle attracts coverage because it is vivid. The systemic error lies elsewhere: officials ceded power willingly, benefited while the arrangement worked and discovered their exhaustion only when the political bill appeared likely to reach them.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: Trump's scorched-earth feud over Daylight Saving Time just turned personal
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened According to AlterNet, Donald Trump escalated his campaign for permanent daylight saving time by publishing Senator Tom Cotton’s personal cellphone number after Cotton blocked the Sunshine Protection Act in the Senate. Trump urged people to contact Cotton and argued that later evening light would benefit golf, tennis, hunting, farming, and PGA Tour events. The House had passed the measure 308–117 on July 14, although the report does not specify the year. Cotton defended his opposit
item.content:encoded:
What happened

According to AlterNet, Donald Trump escalated his campaign for permanent daylight saving time by publishing Senator Tom Cotton’s personal cellphone number after Cotton blocked the Sunshine Protection Act in the Senate. Trump urged people to contact Cotton and argued that later evening light would benefit golf, tennis, hunting, farming, and PGA Tour events.

The House had passed the measure 308–117 on July 14, although the report does not specify the year. Cotton defended his opposition by noting that previous experiments with permanent daylight saving time were repealed after the public experienced extremely late winter sunrises.

AlterNet connects Trump’s position to his golf holdings, reporting that he earned nearly $395 million from activity at 16 courses during the previous year. That financial overlap is relevant, but the article does not establish that personal profit caused his position.

Power, not sunlight

Congress holds the power to set the national clock regime. Trump can pressure lawmakers and mobilize supporters, but senators determine whether the House bill advances. Cotton exercised that institutional authority by preventing a vote or passage, according to the report.

Publishing a senator’s private number turns a policy disagreement into targeted personal pressure. Whatever Cotton’s broader politics, the relevant conduct here is straightforward: he used Senate power to obstruct a bill, and Trump answered by directing public attention toward him personally. That tactic substitutes intimidation and mass harassment risk for an argument on the merits.

The conflict the framing obscures

AlterNet portrays this primarily as Trump sacrificing children for golf revenue. The evidence supplied supports a conflict-of-interest concern, not a proven account of motive. Trump owns golf properties, reported substantial golf-related income, and publicly cited golfers and the PGA Tour as beneficiaries. Those facts warrant scrutiny. They do not, by themselves, prove that enriching his businesses drove the campaign.

The article’s strongest case does not require that leap. A politically powerful businessman is advocating a national policy that could benefit his industry while publicly targeting the senator blocking it. The failure is institutional: lawmakers considering the measure must evaluate public-health evidence and private financial interests, rather than treating presidential pressure as a substitute for either.

The false choice

The public is not limited to permanent daylight saving time or disruptive clock changes forever. The research cited by AlterNet distinguishes permanent daylight time from permanent standard time.

The Canadian Medical Association Journal analysis described morning light as the central signal aligning biological clocks. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine likewise favored standard time, according to the report. Data cited in the article associated later sunrise conditions with reduced sleep, poorer mood, lower productivity, and weaker school performance. Research from K12 estimated that permanent daylight time would leave students commuting in darkness every winter morning in 94 of the country’s 100 largest school districts.

That distinction matters because the slogan “stop changing the clocks” conceals the consequential decision: which clock becomes permanent. A popular complaint about seasonal switching can be used to sell the option friendliest to evening recreation while obscuring the option better aligned with morning light.

Who absorbs the cost

The benefits described are concentrated: more usable evening hours for golf courses, sports organizations, and other recreation businesses. The foreseeable burdens are dispersed among children traveling before sunrise, workers starting early shifts, and drivers operating under greater sleep disruption.

AlterNet cites a 6 percent increase in traffic deaths during the week after the spring clock change, a 24 percent increase in heart attacks on the following morning in one hospital study, and higher injury rates among miners after the transition. Those findings support ending the twice-yearly disruption. They do not establish that permanent daylight time is the safe remedy; the evidence presented points toward permanent standard time instead.

The systemic error

This is how a narrow commercial preference acquires the costume of universal convenience. Industry gains are specific and monetizable. Health, sleep, school performance, and morning safety are fragmented across millions of people who have no comparable lobbying apparatus.

The personal attack on Cotton is not the central policy fact, but it reveals the governing method: concentrate pressure on the institutional obstacle while simplifying the choice offered to everyone else. The deeper failure would be Congress allowing that pressure—and an appealing slogan about ending clock changes—to erase the real question of who receives the extra light and who is sent into the dark.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.

item.title: Fox News delivers humiliating snub to Trump as viewers vanish
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: What happened AlterNet reports that Fox News has stopped routinely airing President Donald Trump’s campaign rallies in full, instead showing selected portions. Trump complained that Fox was neglecting his rallies, criticized its interviews with Democratic candidates, and urged supporters to watch Right Side Broadcasting Network instead. The shift coincided with an October ratings decline. Nielsen figures cited by AlterNet showed Fox’s total-day audience down 27 percent from October 2025 to an av
item.content:encoded:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Fox News has stopped routinely airing President Donald Trump’s campaign rallies in full, instead showing selected portions. Trump complained that Fox was neglecting his rallies, criticized its interviews with Democratic candidates, and urged supporters to watch Right Side Broadcasting Network instead.

The shift coincided with an October ratings decline. Nielsen figures cited by AlterNet showed Fox’s total-day audience down 27 percent from October 2025 to an average of 1.1 million viewers, while its audience aged 25 to 54 fell 32 percent to 98,000—the network’s lowest result in that demographic in 25 years. Weekday prime-time viewership fell 28 percent to roughly 2 million, though Fox remained the most-watched cable news network.

CNN analyst Brian Stelter suggested that some conservative viewers may be tuning out because of dissatisfaction with Trump’s handling of the Epstein files, the war in Iran, and gasoline prices. The ratings do not establish that explanation, nor do they prove how those viewers intended to vote in the November 3 midterm elections.

Fox still holds the switch

Calling this a “snub” reduces an institutional decision to celebrity melodrama. Fox controls access to the largest cable-news audience. Trump can complain, but Fox executives decide which rallies receive uninterrupted distribution, which candidates enter its studios, and what its viewers encounter as politically important.

That is not humiliation so much as a renegotiation of power. Fox once treated Trump’s speeches as programming that could command attention. Now it is editing them for selected moments while interviewing more Democratic Senate and gubernatorial candidates. Whether the motive is electoral positioning, audience expansion, or simple ratings management is not established. The exercise of gatekeeping power is.

A partnership built on utility

Fox’s change does not make the network an adversary of Trump or an independent corrective to him. AlterNet reports that it remains larger than CNN and MS NOW combined. Reducing rally coverage while preserving that dominance looks less like a rupture than an institution adjusting a profitable political product whose performance has weakened.

Trump’s response exposes the transaction. He expects favorable exposure from a network that has long supplied it; when Fox withholds some of that exposure, he directs supporters toward a more compliant outlet. The dispute is over control of the audience, not a newly discovered commitment to neutral journalism.

Ratings are evidence, not a ballot

The sharp decline is politically relevant, especially before a major election when political audiences might ordinarily grow. But the article leans too heavily on the possibility that Fox’s losses measure conservative disillusionment with Trump.

They may. They may also reflect changes in viewing habits, dissatisfaction with Fox, competition from other right-wing media, or factors the reporting does not identify. The figures document fewer viewers, not their reasons, partisan loyalties, or voting plans. Presenting a plausible interpretation as an “early indication” is defensible only if the uncertainty remains visible.

The misdirection of personal drama

The “humiliating blow” framing centers Trump’s wounded status and obscures the more consequential development: a dominant media institution is deciding how much political reach a president receives and recalibrating when the audience stops responding.

That framing also turns viewers into an atmospheric force—people who simply “vanish.” They are making choices, even if the available data cannot explain them. Fox is making choices too. Treating the story as a feud between a politician and his television ally hides the network’s agency and the commercial incentives governing political visibility.

The system follows attention

This episode reveals a media system in which political loyalty lasts only as long as it remains useful. Fox amplified Trump when his rallies held viewers. As that value appears to decline, it is trimming the product, testing other guests, and protecting its market position.

The larger pattern is not that cable news has corrected itself. It is that concentrated media power can build political authority, ration access to it, and then market the withdrawal as a change in the public mood. The audience numbers matter. The institution deciding what those numbers mean—and whose microphone stays live—matters more.

Source: AlterNet

This isn’t a glitch.
It’s the design.

Written and published by Paulo Santos for Systemic Error.
